questions.title: Build a dynamic RLS role with a bidirectional mapping table
questions.prompt: Design and write a dynamic RLS role for a model where a ManagerTerritoryMap table (ManagerUPN, TerritoryID) sits on the 'one' side of a relationship to DimSalesTerritory, which itself relates to FactInternetSales. A manager should see only sales for their assigned territory. Write the role expression, specify exactly which relationship setting needs to change and why, and state the one constraint that setting is subject to.
questions.modelAnswer: The role itself is a single dynamic filter on the mapping table: [ManagerUPN] = USERPRINCIPALNAME(). The problem is relationship direction: by default an RLS filter only flows one way across a relationship regardless of the relationship's own cross-filter direction setting, and ManagerTerritoryMap sits on the side that needs the filter to flow outward — through DimSalesTerritory and on to FactInternetSales — not just filter itself. Left at the default, the filter on ManagerTerritoryMap would narrow that table down to the signed-in manager's row but never propagate out to actually restrict which FactInternetSales rows are visible. The fix is enabling 'Apply security filter in both directions' on the relationship between ManagerTerritoryMap and DimSalesTerritory, which lets the RLS filter — specifically, and only the RLS filter, not ordinary report filtering — flow in both directions across that relationship. The constraint to flag before enabling it: if DimSalesTerritory (or whichever table sits in the middle) already participates in more than one bidirectional relationship, this option can only be enabled on one of them — you can't bidirectionally-filter-for-security on two relationships touching the same table simultaneously. It's also worth validating with Test as role before trusting it, and testing for a real performance regression, since bidirectional security filtering has a genuine query-time cost on a large fact table like FactInternetSales.
questions.professionalAnswer: The role expression itself is simple — ManagerUPN equals USERPRINCIPALNAME() on the mapping table. The real work is getting the filter to actually reach FactInternetSales, because by default RLS filters are one-directional regardless of how the relationship's normal cross-filtering is configured. Since my mapping table sits upstream of DimSalesTerritory, I need to turn on 'Apply security filter in both directions' on that specific relationship — that's the one setting that lets the security filter, specifically, propagate the direction I need. The thing I always check before flipping that switch: does DimSalesTerritory already have another bidirectional relationship elsewhere in the model? Because if it does, I can only enable this option on one of them — Power BI won't let me stack it. After that, I validate with Test as role and I genuinely load-test it, because bidirectional security filtering isn't free — on a fact table this size it can show up as real query latency, and 'technically correct but three seconds slower' isn't a result I'd ship without flagging it first.
commonMistakes: Writing the role expression but leaving the relationship as single-directional, so the filter never reaches the fact table
Enabling bidirectional security filtering on every relationship touching the table instead of checking the one-per-table constraint
Not load-testing the performance cost before deploying
Confusing bidirectional security filtering with ordinary bidirectional cross-filtering (a different, unrelated setting)
keyPoints: Dynamic RLS role expression: [ManagerUPN] = USERPRINCIPALNAME()
RLS filters are single-directional by default regardless of relationship cross-filter mode
Apply security filter in both directions propagates the RLS filter specifically
A table can only have this setting enabled on one of its relationships if it has multiple bidirectional ones
Performance cost must be tested, especially on large fact tables

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct dynamic RLS role expression
Correctly identifies the need for bidirectional security filtering and why
States the one-relationship-per-table constraint accurately
Mentions validation (Test as role) and performance cost

questions.title: Write the subscriber query for a data-driven subscription
questions.prompt: Write the T-SQL query a data-driven subscription's dataset would run against a subscriber roster table to email a 'RegionalSalesSummary' report to every active subscriber, each with their own region passed in as a report parameter. Explain how the columns you select map to the subscription wizard's delivery fields, and why validating this query in SSMS first matters more here than for an ordinary report dataset.
questions.modelAnswer: The query needs to return exactly the columns the subscription wizard's delivery and parameter fields need mapped: an email address column for the To field, and a region value column for the report's region parameter. Each returned row becomes one delivery — the report runs once per row, with that row's region value substituted into the parameter — so the WHERE clause (filtering to active subscribers) and any JOIN logic directly determine how many deliveries fire, not just who they go to. In the wizard, after the dataset validates, each delivery field's Source of value is set to 'Get value from dataset' with Value/field pointing at ToEmailAddress for the To column and RegionName for the report's Region parameter; everything else (subject, include-report flag) can stay literal. Validating in SSMS first matters more here than for a normal report dataset because a mistake in an ordinary dataset just shows wrong numbers on one report render that a user can immediately see and flag — a mistake in a data-driven subscription's query (say, a missing WHERE IsActive = 1 filter, or a JOIN that fans out and duplicates rows) silently generates the wrong number of emails, to the wrong people, unattended, often overnight, with nobody watching it happen. Catching a row-count or duplicate-row problem in SSMS before pasting the query into the wizard is the only realistic way to prevent that.
questions.professionalAnswer: I write this exactly like I would for any join, but I think about it differently: every row this returns is a real email going to a real person, unattended. So first I run it in SSMS and sanity-check two things — the row count matches how many active subscribers I actually expect, and there are no accidental duplicate rows from a fan-out join, because a duplicate row means someone gets the same report twice. Only after that do I paste it into the subscription wizard, where ToEmailAddress maps to the To field's Value/field and RegionName maps to the Region report parameter, both set to 'Get value from dataset.' The reason I treat this more carefully than an ordinary report dataset is that an ordinary report's mistake is visible immediately — the user sees wrong numbers and tells me. A subscription query's mistake is invisible until it's already fired, at 6 a.m., to however many people the bad row count produced — there's no user in the loop to catch it in the moment.
questions.example:
SELECT
    s.EmailAddress AS ToEmailAddress,
    s.RegionName
FROM dbo.SubscriberRoster AS s
WHERE s.IsActive = 1
  AND s.ReportCode = 'RegionalSalesSummary';
commonMistakes: Forgetting a WHERE IsActive = 1 filter, emailing deactivated or departed subscribers
Letting a JOIN fan out and duplicate rows, sending the same report twice to the same person
Not validating the query in SSMS before pasting it into the wizard
Returning extra columns the wizard has no field to map, instead of exactly what delivery needs
keyPoints: Each returned row produces one independent report delivery
Column names map directly to wizard fields via 'Get value from dataset'
Row count and duplicate-row risk are the two things to check before trusting the query
A subscriber query's mistake is invisible until it already fired, unlike an ordinary report dataset

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Produces a correct, working subscriber query
Correctly explains the column-to-wizard-field mapping
Explains why rows directly control delivery count
Articulates why SSMS validation matters more here than for a normal dataset

questions.title: Design a cache refresh plan for a daily sales dashboard
questions.prompt: A company-wide sales dashboard report is opened by roughly 200 people between 7:00 and 9:00 AM every weekday, and its underlying query takes 90 seconds to run. Design the caching configuration you'd set up — execution mode, cache expiration, and refresh plan — and justify why a report snapshot would be the wrong tool here even though it's also an option.
questions.modelAnswer: This report is exactly the case caching is built for: shared, frequently viewed, by many different people, in a narrow window. The configuration: set execution mode to 'Cache copies of this report and use them when available,' with Cache Expiration set to expire on a schedule (end of business day) rather than a short fixed-minutes window, since the data only needs to be current once per day for this use case. Critically, add a Cache Refresh Plan scheduled for roughly 6:45 AM — 15 minutes before the first wave of viewers arrives — so the 90-second query already ran and the cache is warm before any of the 200 people request the report; without a refresh plan, caching still helps (only the first of 200 users pays the 90-second cost), but that first unlucky user still waits 90 seconds, and a refresh plan eliminates even that. A report snapshot is the wrong tool here specifically because a snapshot is meant for reports that should run on a schedule independent of anyone viewing them — which caching with a refresh plan already achieves — while also locking the report to running only against pregenerated snapshots, which removes the option of ever seeing live data that day if someone genuinely needs it refreshed sooner. Snapshots are the right call for a report whose query is a burden the data source shouldn't bear during business hours at all, or where the report's output doesn't qualify for caching (per-user data, Windows-integrated security); this report has neither of those constraints, so caching plus a refresh plan is simpler, equally fast, and more flexible.
questions.professionalAnswer: Given 200 people hitting this in a two-hour window with a 90-second query, caching is the obvious lever, but I wouldn't stop at just turning caching on — I'd add a refresh plan timed for about 6:45, ahead of the rush, so the cache is already warm and literally nobody pays that 90 seconds, not even the first person in. Expiration I'd set to end-of-day rather than some short minutes window, since this data only genuinely needs to refresh once a day for this audience. Somebody will inevitably ask 'why not just snapshot it instead' — and my answer is that a snapshot buys us nothing extra here. The whole point of a snapshot is running independent of viewers, but my refresh plan already does that. What a snapshot does cost us is flexibility — it locks the report to only ever showing that pregenerated data, so if someone genuinely needs a live number later in the day, we can't get it without switching modes. Since this report has no per-user data and no Windows-integrated security blocking caching in the first place, caching plus a refresh plan is the simpler, equally fast, more flexible choice.
commonMistakes: Choosing a report snapshot by default without checking whether caching plus a refresh plan already solves the problem
Setting cache expiration to a short fixed-minutes window instead of matching the real freshness requirement
Forgetting to add a cache refresh plan, leaving the first user of the day to pay the full query cost
Not checking whether the report even qualifies for caching (per-user data or Windows-integrated security would disqualify it)
keyPoints: Caching is correct for shared, frequently-viewed reports — exactly this scenario
A cache refresh plan proactively warms the cache before the real traffic arrives
Expiration should match the real freshness requirement, not default to a short window
Snapshots solve a different problem: independence from viewers and data-source protection, not needed here
Per-user data or Windows-integrated security would disqualify caching/snapshots entirely

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct execution-mode and expiration configuration for the scenario
Includes a cache refresh plan timed ahead of real usage
Correctly justifies why a snapshot would be the wrong tool here
Notes the disqualifying conditions for caching in general

questions.title: Fix a model where RLS and USERELATIONSHIP() collide
questions.prompt: A sales model has dynamic RLS enabled via a bidirectional-filtered mapping table, and a 'Ship Date Sales' measure that activates the inactive ship-date relationship with USERELATIONSHIP(). Since RLS went live, that measure throws unexpected errors for RLS-restricted users, though it worked fine before. Diagnose the collision and redesign the model so both features coexist.
questions.modelAnswer: USERELATIONSHIP() activates a normally-inactive relationship for the scope of one measure's evaluation, and RLS with bidirectional security filtering is simultaneously trying to propagate its own filter across the model's active relationships. Those two mechanisms can conflict: activating an alternate relationship inside a measure while a bidirectional RLS filter is also trying to flow through the model's relationship graph can produce an ambiguous or unsupported filter-propagation path, which is exactly the documented edge case — RLS enabled alongside USERELATIONSHIP() inside a measure can trigger unexpected errors. The fix is not to disable RLS; it's to redesign around the conflict. The most robust fix is to stop relying on USERELATIONSHIP() for the ship-date role entirely: materialize ship-date sales as its own bridge/fact perspective with a direct, always-active relationship to DimDate on the ship-date key (for example, a separate fact table or a pre-aggregated table keyed specifically to ship date), so the 'Ship Date Sales' measure no longer needs to activate an alternate relationship at query time at all — it just sums against a model-level relationship that's already active, which RLS's bidirectional filter can propagate through normally. A lighter-weight alternative, if a full redesign isn't feasible immediately, is to scope USERELATIONSHIP() usage to reports/visuals that RLS-restricted Viewers don't actually use, and keep it for internal, unrestricted audiences only — but that's a workaround, not a fix, and should be tracked as technical debt.
questions.professionalAnswer: What's happening is two features stepping on each other: USERELATIONSHIP is temporarily rerouting the filter path for one measure, and bidirectional RLS is trying to push its own filter across the model's relationships at the same time, and that combination isn't reliably supported — it's a known collision, not a bug in our formula. My instinct isn't to disable RLS to make the error go away; it's to stop depending on USERELATIONSHIP for this specific role. I'd redesign so ship-date sales has its own real, always-active relationship to the date table — a dedicated table or perspective keyed on ship date — so that measure just sums through a normal active relationship instead of activating an alternate one at query time. Once it's not fighting with RLS over the relationship path, the error goes away and RLS's bidirectional filter can propagate the way it's supposed to. If I genuinely can't redesign the model today, I'd at least scope that measure away from any report RLS-restricted users touch, and flag it as debt — but that's a stopgap, and I'd say so out loud to the team, not quietly ship it as the real fix.
commonMistakes: Disabling RLS or bidirectional filtering to 'fix' the error instead of redesigning the measure
Not recognizing USERELATIONSHIP + bidirectional RLS as a known collision
Leaving the workaround (scoping the measure away from RLS users) undocumented as permanent instead of tracked debt
Assuming the error is a formula bug rather than a model-design conflict
keyPoints: USERELATIONSHIP activates an inactive relationship for one measure's scope
Bidirectional RLS filtering across the same relationship graph can conflict with that activation
The documented fix is redesigning around model-level relationships, not disabling RLS
A dedicated role-playing table/relationship avoids needing USERELATIONSHIP at query time
A scoping workaround is acceptable only as tracked technical debt, not a final fix

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly diagnoses the USERELATIONSHIP/RLS collision
Proposes a real model redesign rather than disabling RLS
Provides a working example contrasting the broken and fixed approach
Flags any interim workaround as debt, not a permanent solution

questions.title: A refresh schedule silently stopped running
questions.prompt: A finance semantic model's nightly refresh hasn't actually run in six days, but nobody noticed until a VP asked why the numbers looked stale. No one changed the schedule. Diagnose the most likely cause, explain why it happened silently, and design a monitoring fix so this specific failure mode can't go unnoticed again.
questions.modelAnswer: The leading suspect is the four-failures rule: Power BI automatically disables a scheduled refresh after four consecutive failures, with no warning beyond the failure emails themselves — and if those emails were going to an account nobody monitors, or had been removed from the semantic model's notification settings, the disablement would be completely silent to the team even though the mechanism itself worked exactly as designed. Something caused the first failure six-plus days ago (an outdated gateway, expired stored credentials, or a source schema change breaking a Processing Error: Type Mismatch) — within four attempts, the schedule turned itself off, and refresh simply stopped with no further failures to even generate more emails. The fix has two layers. First, root-cause the original failure using refresh history (status, duration, error per attempt) and confirm the gateway version and source schema haven't drifted. Second — more importantly for preventing a repeat — stop relying on a toggle anyone can silently lose track of: set up monitoring that doesn't depend on someone reading an email, such as a scheduled check (via admin APIs or a lightweight automated job) that alerts a shared channel or ticketing system whenever a model's refresh-enabled state flips to off, or whenever a model's last-successful-refresh timestamp exceeds its expected cadence. Relying purely on per-user failure emails is exactly the single point of failure that let this go unnoticed for six days.
questions.professionalAnswer: My first guess, before even opening refresh history, is the four-failures rule — Power BI will auto-disable a schedule after four failures in a row, and the only notice is a failure email, which is easy for an email filter or an inactive recipient to swallow completely. So I'd check refresh history first to find what the original failure actually was — gateway version, expired credentials, a schema change — fix that, then flip the schedule back on. But fixing today's incident isn't the real deliverable here; the real gap is that we had no way to know a refresh had silently turned itself off for six days. So I'd set up a monitoring check that doesn't depend on a human reading an email — something that polls refresh status or the model's refresh-enabled flag and posts to a channel the team actually watches the moment either one looks wrong. The failure-email mechanism did exactly what it was built to do; the actual bug here is organizational, not technical — we built a single point of failure around a notification nobody was reliably watching.
commonMistakes: Assuming someone must have manually disabled the schedule
Fixing the immediate failure cause without addressing why six days passed unnoticed
Relying solely on refresh-failure emails as the only monitoring mechanism going forward
Not checking refresh history to find the actual original failure cause
keyPoints: Four consecutive failures auto-disables a scheduled refresh with no further warning
Refresh history shows status/duration/error for every attempt — the starting point for root cause
Common original causes: outdated gateway, expired credentials, source schema change
The real fix is monitoring that doesn't rely on a human reading an email
Re-enabling requires fixing the root cause first, then manually flipping the schedule back on

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies the four-failures rule as the likely mechanism
Uses refresh history to reason about the original root cause
Proposes a monitoring fix independent of per-user email
Distinguishes the immediate fix from the systemic one

questions.title: Dynamic RLS that worked at 50K rows times out at 50M
questions.prompt: A dynamic RLS model built on USERPRINCIPALNAME() and a user-mapping table performed fine in UAT against a 50,000-row fact table. In production against the real 50-million-row fact table, every report using that role times out. Diagnose the likely causes and redesign the model so dynamic RLS scales.
questions.modelAnswer: At 50M rows, several things that were invisible at 50K become the actual bottleneck. First: if the mapping table joins on a text column (email/UPN) rather than an integer surrogate key, every row-level filter evaluation is doing string comparisons across a much larger table — string joins and string-based filters are measurably more expensive than integer-key joins at scale, and that cost scales with fact-table size. Second: if bidirectional security filtering is enabled to make the RLS filter reach the fact table, that setting has a real, documented performance cost that's negligible at 50K rows and very much not negligible at 50M — it's effectively forcing a cross-filtering join pattern on every query, and on a large fact table this multiplies with bidirectional filtering's own join overhead. Third: if the mapping table or any ALLEXCEPT/context-transition logic used alongside RLS is re-evaluated per row rather than being precomputed, that cost scales linearly (or worse) with fact table size. The redesign: (1) replace the email/UPN join with an integer ManagerKey surrogate key — map UPN to ManagerKey once in a small dimension, and filter on the integer key, not the string; (2) re-examine whether bidirectional security filtering is actually required, or whether the mapping table can instead sit directly against a dimension already on the correct side of a single-directional relationship to the fact table, avoiding the bidirectional cost altogether; (3) consider a composite model with an aggregation table for the common high-level views report users actually hit most, so RLS-filtered queries against summarized data don't need to touch all 50M detail rows for every visual; (4) validate the fix with Test as role against production-scale data, not just the UAT-scale dataset, since the whole point is that this bug only appears at real volume.
questions.professionalAnswer: This is the classic 'worked in UAT, fell over in prod' story, and the giveaway is always scale-dependent cost that was invisible on a small dataset. My first two suspects: are we joining the mapping table on the UPN string instead of an integer key, and is bidirectional security filtering turned on? Both of those have a real cost that's basically free at 50,000 rows and genuinely expensive at 50 million — string joins scale worse than integer joins, and bidirectional filtering is documented as a real performance hit on large fact tables specifically. So my redesign is: swap the string join for an integer ManagerKey surrogate, re-examine whether we actually still need bidirectional filtering once the model's shaped a bit differently, and if the reports people actually hit are mostly summary-level, I'd add an aggregation table so those common queries aren't scanning all 50 million detail rows under an RLS filter every time. And critically, I wouldn't sign off on this fix against UAT data again — the bug only shows up at real volume, so the fix only gets validated at real volume too.
commonMistakes: Assuming RLS itself is inherently the slow part, rather than how the mapping join is keyed
Keeping a string-based join at any real scale instead of an integer surrogate key
Not reconsidering whether bidirectional security filtering is still necessary after a redesign
Re-testing the fix only against the small UAT dataset instead of production-scale data
keyPoints: String-keyed joins scale worse than integer-keyed joins as fact table size grows
Bidirectional security filtering has a real, documented performance cost at scale
An aggregation table can keep common summary queries off the full 50M-row detail scan
Any fix must be validated against production-scale data, not the original UAT dataset

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies scale-dependent causes (string join, bidirectional cost)
Proposes a concrete redesign (surrogate key, relationship reshape, aggregation)
Recognizes why the bug was invisible at UAT scale
Insists on production-scale validation of the fix

questions.title: One report is slow — is it the report, or the server?
questions.prompt: Users report that 'reports are slow' on the production report server. Before touching any query, lay out the diagnostic process you'd use to determine whether this is an infrastructure problem affecting everything, or one specific report, and explain what you'd do differently depending on the answer.
questions.modelAnswer: The first and most important diagnostic question is binary: is every report slow, or just this one? The answer points to a completely different fix, so I wouldn't touch a single query before answering it. I'd go straight to the execution log (the ExecutionLog3 view, or a report built on top of it — Top 10 Longest Running, Top 10 Most Executed, executions per day/hour) rather than trusting anecdote, because 'reports are slow' from a handful of users is exactly the kind of vague signal that execution-log data turns into an actual answer. If the data shows broad, even degradation across many different reports, the problem is infrastructure, not any one report's design — under-provisioned hardware, the report server and its database competing for resources on the same box, or genuine overall load exceeding what a single instance can handle. The fix there is scale-out: additional report server instances sharing one database, with load balanced across them, or separating the report server and database onto different machines if they're currently colocated. If instead Top 10 Longest Running clearly isolates one or two specific reports while everything else performs normally, the fix lives inside those reports, starting with dataset query efficiency — filtering, sorting, and aggregating at the source instead of inside the report, and checking for expressions re-evaluated per row inside tables or matrices. Only after query tuning is exhausted would caching or a snapshot even enter the conversation, since those are multipliers on an already-efficient report, not a substitute for fixing an inefficient one. I'd measure before and after with the same execution log, so the fix is validated with a number, not a feeling.
questions.professionalAnswer: Before I touch anything, I go to the execution log, not the complaint. 'Reports are slow' from a few users doesn't tell me if this is one report or the whole server, and that distinction changes everything about what I'd do next. ExecutionLog3 — or a report built on it, Top 10 Longest Running specifically — gives me a real answer instead of a guess. If the slowness is spread evenly across lots of different reports, that's infrastructure: the server's under-provisioned, or the database and report server are fighting for resources on the same box, and the real fix is scale-out, not touching any individual report's design. If it's really one or two specific reports showing up at the top of that list while everything else is fine, then I go straight to that report's dataset query — filtering and aggregating at the source instead of pulling everything and doing it in the report body — before I ever reach for caching. Caching and snapshots are a multiplier on an already-efficient report, not a fix for an inefficient one, so I don't want to mask a bad query with a cache and call it solved. And either way, I pull the same execution-log numbers again after the fix, so I'm reporting back a measured improvement, not just 'it feels faster.'
commonMistakes: Jumping straight to caching or a snapshot without first tuning the underlying query
Trusting user anecdote over execution-log data to decide scope
Assuming 'slow' automatically means infrastructure, without checking whether it's isolated to specific reports
Not measuring before/after with the execution log, leaving the fix unvalidated
keyPoints: First diagnostic question: every report, or just one?
ExecutionLog3 / Top 10 Longest Running turns anecdote into real data
Broad slowness points to infrastructure/scale-out; isolated slowness points to query tuning
Query tuning comes before caching or snapshots, not after
Measure before and after the fix using the same execution-log data

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Leads with the every-report-vs-one-report diagnostic question
Uses execution log / ExecutionLog3 data rather than anecdote
Correctly differentiates the infrastructure fix from the query-tuning fix
Insists on before/after measurement

questions.title: One gateway node offline breaks forty workspaces
questions.prompt: A single on-premises data gateway, installed in personal mode years ago on a departed employee's workstation, silently went offline over the weekend. Monday morning, scheduled refreshes fail across roughly 40 workspaces tenant-wide, and nobody can agree on why so much broke from one machine. Diagnose the architectural root cause and redesign the gateway setup so this can't happen again.
questions.modelAnswer: The root cause isn't really 'a machine went offline' — it's that a personal-mode gateway, which is explicitly single-user and non-shareable, somehow ended up as a load-bearing dependency for 40 workspaces across the tenant, almost certainly because semantic models across many teams were pointed at it opportunistically over time with nobody tracking that concentration. Personal mode exists for a solo learner or individual's own machine precisely because it isn't meant to be shared infrastructure — once it became exactly that, the organization had, unknowingly, built a single point of failure with no redundancy, no shared administration, and ownership tied to one person's workstation that nobody re-pointed when that person left. The fix is architectural, not a quick restart: migrate every semantic model currently depending on that personal-mode gateway onto a standard on-premises data gateway, which supports multiple users, multiple data sources, and — critically — can be clustered, with multiple gateway instances installed and registered under the same cluster name for high availability, so one machine going offline doesn't take down everything behind it. Gateway administration should move to a small group of named gateway admins (not a single individual's personal account), and semantic model owners should be audited and documented so 'which gateway does this depend on, and who owns it' is answerable without an incident. Going forward, gateway health should be monitored proactively — not discovered via a wave of Monday-morning refresh failures — and any new on-premises connection request should be evaluated against whether it belongs on the shared standard gateway cluster from day one, not bolted onto whatever machine happens to be convenient.
questions.professionalAnswer: The uncomfortable truth here is that the real root cause isn't the gateway going offline — gateways go offline — it's that a personal-mode gateway, which is explicitly not supposed to be shared, somehow became load-bearing infrastructure for 40 workspaces, and nobody noticed that creeping dependency until it broke. That's an architecture failure, not a one-time outage. My fix is to migrate everything off that personal-mode gateway onto a proper standard gateway, and specifically a clustered one — multiple instances registered under the same cluster name — so a single machine going offline is a non-event instead of a tenant-wide incident. I'd also fix the ownership gap: gateway administration needs to belong to a named team, not one person's workstation, and we need an actual inventory of which semantic models depend on which gateway, so this conversation next time takes five minutes instead of a morning of finger-pointing. And I'd put monitoring in front of gateway health going forward, because the way we found out about this — a wave of failed refreshes Monday morning — is the worst possible way to find out about it.
commonMistakes: Treating this as a one-time outage to restart rather than an architectural single point of failure
Not recognizing that personal-mode gateways are explicitly unsuited to being shared, load-bearing infrastructure
Migrating to a standard gateway without clustering it, leaving the same single-point-of-failure risk
No inventory of which semantic models depend on which gateway, making future incidents equally confusing
keyPoints: Personal-mode gateways are single-user and non-shareable by design — not meant for this load
Standard gateways support multiple users/sources and can be clustered for high availability
Ownership tied to one individual's machine is itself the governance failure
An inventory of model-to-gateway dependency prevents repeat confusion during incidents
Proactive gateway health monitoring beats discovering failure via a wave of refresh errors

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Identifies the architectural root cause (personal-mode gateway as unintended shared infra)
Proposes a standard, clustered gateway redesign for HA
Addresses ownership/governance gap, not just the technical fix
Proposes proactive monitoring going forward

questions.title: Design review: capacity and workspace governance for 3,000 seats
questions.prompt: You're the Power BI architect presenting to a review board for a 3,000-seat enterprise tenant. Design the capacity, workspace, and governance model across dev/test/prod, including the Premium-vs-Fabric capacity sizing tradeoff, and explain specifically how you'd prevent one bad dataset refresh from starving the entire capacity for everyone else.
questions.modelAnswer: Workspace/environment structure: separate workspaces (and ideally separate capacities or at least separate capacity-assigned pools) for dev, test, and prod, so a developer's experimental semantic model never competes for the same compute as a production dashboard the CFO is watching live. Role discipline follows Lesson 69's four roles strictly: a small platform-governance group holds Admin everywhere; day-to-day builders get Contributor in dev/test and a tightly controlled Member/Contributor split in prod; end users consume only through apps, never direct workspace access. Capacity sizing: Fabric (F-SKU) capacities are the modern unit and, since Fabric now houses Power BI alongside data engineering and real-time analytics workloads on shared capacity, they make sense if the organization is likely to adopt other Fabric workloads — otherwise a Premium (P-SKU) capacity is functionally equivalent for pure Power BI use and may be the simpler choice to procure today. Size for peak concurrent refresh-plus-interactive-query load, not average load, since Premium/Fabric capacities enforce a shared compute pool across every workspace assigned to them — undersizing means every workspace on that capacity feels the pain of the busiest one. The core risk — one bad dataset refresh starving the whole capacity — is addressed on three levels: (1) workload management settings on the capacity, which let an admin cap how much of the capacity's resources a given workload (like Dataset refresh) can consume, preventing one workload type from monopolizing everything; (2) capacity-level autoscale (where available) to absorb genuine spikes rather than letting them degrade every other workspace; (3) governance controls on model design itself — refresh timeouts, dataset size limits, and a review gate before a new large or complex model goes onto a shared production capacity, so the 'bad refresh' is caught before deployment rather than mitigated after the fact. I'd also keep at least one workspace's worth of headroom unassigned/reserved so a true outlier incident has somewhere to be isolated rather than immediately re-triggering a capacity-wide incident.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd present this in three layers, because 'capacity planning' actually means three different decisions stacked on top of each other. First, environment separation: dev, test, and prod get their own workspaces, and ideally their own capacity assignment, so an experiment in dev literally cannot compete for compute with a live executive dashboard in prod — that's non-negotiable. Second, the capacity SKU decision: Fabric capacities are where Microsoft's putting their investment, and if we think we'll ever touch other Fabric workloads, I'd go Fabric now rather than migrate later; if we're purely a Power BI shop with no near-term Fabric ambitions, Premium is functionally the same thing today and might be the simpler procurement. Either way, I size for peak concurrent load, not average, because everyone on that capacity shares the same compute pool — undersizing doesn't just slow down the heavy workspace, it slows down everyone. Third, and this is the question I know the board actually cares about: how do we stop one bad refresh from taking everyone down. My answer is workload management settings at the capacity level — we can cap how much of the capacity a given workload type, like dataset refresh, is allowed to consume, so it physically can't eat the whole pool. On top of that, I'd put a review gate in front of any new large model going into production, and keep a sliver of reserved headroom so a genuine outlier incident has somewhere to land instead of immediately becoming everyone's problem.
commonMistakes: Sizing capacity for average load instead of peak concurrent load
Not separating dev/test/prod onto distinct workspace/capacity boundaries
Assuming Premium and Fabric are interchangeable without considering future Fabric workload adoption
Missing workload management settings as the actual control for preventing one workload from starving the capacity
No review gate before large/complex models go into a shared production capacity
keyPoints: Dev/test/prod separation at the workspace and ideally capacity level
Role discipline (Admin/Member/Contributor/Viewer) enforced consistently across environments
Fabric vs Premium is a strategic bet on future Fabric workload adoption, not a pure feature gap today
Capacity sizing must target peak concurrent load across the shared pool
Workload management settings cap per-workload resource consumption to prevent starvation
A pre-deployment review gate catches 'bad refresh' risk before it reaches shared capacity

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Designs a coherent dev/test/prod workspace and role model
Correctly reasons through Premium vs Fabric capacity tradeoffs
Sizes capacity against peak shared-pool load, not average
Proposes a concrete mechanism (workload management) preventing one refresh from starving the capacity
Includes a governance/review-gate layer, not just technical settings

questions.title: Architecture review: 500 branch managers, one 7 AM deadline
questions.prompt: 500 branch managers each need their own filtered report refreshed and delivered before 7:00 AM every business day, from a report server that currently serves the whole company. Present the subscription, caching, and server architecture you'd design so this doesn't melt the report server, including how you'd decide between a data-driven subscription and scale-out, or both.
questions.modelAnswer: This is fundamentally a fan-out problem: one report, 500 personalized deliveries, on a hard deadline, and the architecture has to address both the query load and the rendering/delivery load separately. Delivery mechanism: a single data-driven subscription against a branch-manager roster table is the right tool — the subscriber query returns 500 rows (branch manager email, branch ID), and each row becomes one filtered delivery, exactly matching the requirement without 500 hand-maintained standard subscriptions. But a data-driven subscription firing 500 report executions back-to-back at, say, 6:30 AM is itself a load spike that can overwhelm a single report server instance — this is where caching/snapshot design and scale-out both matter, not as alternatives but as complementary layers. Query efficiency first: the underlying dataset query must filter by branch ID at the source (parameterized dataset), never pull all branches' data and filter in the report, since that cost is paid 500 times. Caching strategy: because each delivery is parameterized per branch, a single cached copy doesn't directly help this report the way it would a shared dashboard — but a cache refresh plan or snapshot on any shared sub-reports/datasets feeding this one (e.g., a shared dataset used across branches) absolutely does, and shared-dataset caching should be used wherever the underlying data is common across branches even if the final rendered output differs. Infrastructure: if 500 renders in a tight pre-7am window exceeds one instance's throughput (validated via the execution log from a load test, not guesswork), this is the textbook scale-out scenario — multiple report server instances sharing one report server database, load-balanced, so the subscription's 500 executions distribute across nodes instead of queuing on one box. Scheduling discipline matters too: stagger the subscription's own trigger window if the architecture allows partial batching, and set the subscriber query's execution to begin early enough (say 5:30-6:00 AM) that even a worst-case per-report render time comfortably clears 7:00 AM with margin, validated against the execution log's actual per-report timing data, not an assumption.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd frame this to the board as two separate problems stacked together: how do we generate 500 personalized deliveries without maintaining 500 subscriptions, and how do we make sure generating 500 reports back-to-back doesn't choke the server right before the deadline that matters most. For the first, a single data-driven subscription against our branch roster table is exactly the tool — one query returns 500 rows, each row is one filtered delivery, and nobody's hand-maintaining a subscription per branch manager. For the second, I don't treat caching and scale-out as competing options, I treat them as different layers of the same fix. Query efficiency comes first, always — the dataset has to filter by branch at the source, not pull everything 500 times. Then, if any data is actually shared across branches, I cache or snapshot that shared piece, because that's real, reusable savings. But the big lever, if a load test shows one server can't render 500 personalized reports before 7, is scale-out — multiple report server instances against the same database, so those 500 executions spread across machines instead of queuing on one. And I wouldn't guess at any of this — I'd load-test against the execution log first, see our actual per-report render time, and schedule the subscription early enough that even a bad morning clears 7 AM with real margin, not by luck.
commonMistakes: Building 500 individual standard subscriptions instead of one data-driven subscription
Assuming caching alone solves a per-branch-personalized report's load problem
Jumping straight to scale-out without first fixing dataset query efficiency
Scheduling the subscription right up against the 7 AM deadline with no tested margin
Not load-testing actual per-report render time before committing to an architecture
keyPoints: A single data-driven subscription is the correct fan-out mechanism for 500 personalized deliveries
Query filtering at the source must happen per-branch, since that cost is paid 500 times
Shared-dataset caching helps only the genuinely shared-across-branches portion of the data
Scale-out (multiple report server instances, one database) addresses raw render throughput, not query design
Scheduling margin must be based on measured execution-log render times, not assumption

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly selects a data-driven subscription as the fan-out mechanism
Separates query-efficiency, caching, and scale-out as complementary layers
Ties the design to measured load/execution-log data rather than assumption
Produces a deadline-safe scheduling plan with real margin

questions.title: Mentoring a report developer who keeps shipping slow reports
questions.prompt: A report developer on your team keeps shipping reports with the same problems: unfiltered datasets, the same complex expression repeated in five textboxes, and no formatting. Users complain they're slow and sloppy, but the developer is defensive when you bring it up in front of the team. How do you handle this as their lead?
questions.modelAnswer: The first fix is procedural, not personal: I stop giving this feedback in front of the team. Public correction on a recurring pattern reads as public criticism regardless of intent, and it's already produced defensiveness, which shuts down exactly the learning conversation I need to have. I'd move this to a private 1:1, and reframe it from 'you keep doing this wrong' to a specific, teachable pattern: 'let's walk through why a report with an unfiltered dataset and a repeated expression costs more than it needs to, using one of your actual reports as the example.' I'd use Lesson 37's own diagnostic framing with them directly — filter at the source, don't pull everything and filter inside the report; a repeated expression in five textboxes gets evaluated five times, move it to a calculated field or the dataset; measure the before/after with the execution log so the lesson lands as a number, not just my opinion. I'd also ask what's driving the pattern before assuming it's carelessness — deadline pressure, not knowing the execution log exists, or genuinely not having been taught dataset-level filtering are three very different root causes requiring different mentoring. I'd set a concrete, checkable standard going forward (a lightweight pre-publish checklist: source-filtered datasets, no fully duplicated expressions, formatted output) and review their next two or three reports against it privately, giving credit when it improves rather than only flagging when it doesn't. If after real coaching and a fair runway the pattern continues, that becomes a documented performance conversation — but that's a last resort, not a first move, and it only happens after I've actually taught the skill, not just criticized its absence.
questions.professionalAnswer: Honestly, the first thing I'd fix is my own behavior — if I've been correcting this in front of the team, that's on me, and it's probably why they're defensive instead of receptive. I'd take it to a 1:1 and reframe the whole conversation: not 'you keep doing this wrong,' but 'let's actually walk through one of your reports and look at why this costs more than it needs to.' I'd use the same diagnostic I'd use on myself — is the dataset filtering at the source, is this expression getting evaluated five separate times instead of once, what does the execution log actually show before and after. I want the lesson to land as a number they can see, not my opinion of their work. I'd also genuinely ask what's going on before assuming it's carelessness — are they under deadline pressure, do they just not know the execution log is even a tool they have access to? Those get completely different responses from me. Then I'd give them something concrete to work against — a short pre-publish checklist — and actually look at their next couple of reports privately and tell them when it's better, not just when it isn't. If none of that moves the needle after a real runway, that's a different, more formal conversation — but I don't skip straight to that just because the first attempt in front of the team went badly.
commonMistakes: Continuing to raise the issue in front of the team instead of moving to a private conversation
Assuming carelessness without asking what's actually driving the pattern
Giving vague feedback ('be more careful') instead of a specific, teachable technical standard
Jumping to a formal performance conversation before genuinely coaching the skill
Not giving credit when the developer's next reports actually improve
keyPoints: Move recurring correction to a private setting, not in front of the team
Reframe feedback around a specific, teachable technical pattern, not a character judgment
Use objective data (execution log) to make the lesson concrete, not just opinion
Diagnose the root cause (pressure, skill gap, habit) before choosing the coaching approach
Escalate to a formal performance conversation only after real coaching and a fair runway

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Recognizes and corrects the public-feedback mistake first
Proposes concrete, technically specific coaching grounded in real diagnostics
Investigates root cause before assuming intent
Describes a fair, staged path to escalation if coaching doesn't work

questions.title: Leading the incident bridge: RLS exposed the wrong region's data
questions.prompt: A regional manager reports they can see another region's sales figures in a production dashboard that's supposed to be restricted by dynamic RLS. This is a real data-exposure incident, not a bug report. Walk through how you lead the incident response in the first hour, and what you do differently afterward.
questions.modelAnswer: In the first hour, containment comes before root-causing. I'd immediately check whether the affected workspace/report can be pulled from general access or the semantic model's access temporarily restricted while we investigate — stopping further exposure matters more than understanding it in the first ten minutes. In parallel, I'd scope the blast radius with specific questions, not vague ones: which users are affected, is it one region seeing one other region or a broader leak, and is this isolated to one report or does it affect every report on the same semantic model (Lesson 83's note that RLS filters the whole semantic model, not one page, makes this a real question to answer, not assume). Root-cause candidates I'd check in order, because they're the documented failure modes: is the affected user actually a workspace Viewer, or did they get promoted to Contributor/Member at some point, since RLS silently doesn't apply above Viewer; does the user-mapping table's UPN format actually match what USERPRINCIPALNAME() returns in the service, since Desktop and service can format identity differently; and is a bidirectional-filtering relationship change or a recent model republish the likely trigger, checking recent publish history for timing correlation. I'd communicate status honestly and promptly to the affected manager and to leadership — what we know, what we don't yet, and what's been contained — rather than going quiet until we have a full answer, since a data-exposure incident that looks like silence looks worse than one being actively managed. Afterward: a written incident review covering exact root cause, why Test as role (or whatever validation step existed) didn't catch it, and a concrete process fix — likely requiring Test as role validation as a mandatory, logged gate before any RLS-affecting change reaches production, not an optional best practice. I'd also push for periodic re-validation of RLS roles, not just at initial build, since workspace role creep (a Viewer quietly promoted to Contributor) is exactly the kind of drift that goes unnoticed until an incident surfaces it.
questions.professionalAnswer: My first move isn't diagnosis, it's containment — can we restrict access to that report or semantic model right now while we figure out what happened, because stopping the exposure matters more in minute ten than understanding it does. Once that's moving, I scope it precisely: who's affected, is this one leaked region or several, and does it touch every report on this semantic model or just one — because RLS applies at the semantic-model level, so I treat 'just one report' as a question to verify, not an assumption. Then I work the known failure modes in order, because this isn't the first time anyone's hit these: is the affected person actually a Viewer, or did they get bumped to Contributor at some point and RLS silently stopped applying to them; does our mapping table's email format actually match what the service returns for USERPRINCIPALNAME, because that mismatch is the single most common reason dynamic RLS misbehaves; and did something change recently — a republish, a relationship edit — that lines up with when this started. I keep the affected manager and leadership updated honestly as I go, even with partial information, because silence during a data exposure reads worse than an honest 'here's what we know so far.' Afterward, the real deliverable isn't just the fix — it's making sure Test as role, or whatever validation step should have caught this, becomes a mandatory, logged gate before anything RLS-related ships again, and that we're periodically re-checking role assignments, because a Viewer quietly becoming a Contributor is exactly the kind of drift nobody notices until it's an incident.
commonMistakes: Starting with root-cause investigation before containing further exposure
Assuming the leak is isolated to one report without checking the whole semantic model
Not checking the affected user's actual workspace role first (Viewer vs Contributor/Member)
Going quiet during the incident instead of communicating partial findings honestly
Treating the fix as complete without adding a mandatory pre-production validation gate afterward
keyPoints: Containment precedes root-causing in a real data-exposure incident
RLS applies at the semantic-model level — check all reports on that model, not just the one reported
Check whether the affected user is actually a Viewer; role promotion silently defeats RLS
UPN/email format mismatch between Desktop and service is a documented, common root cause
Post-incident fix must include a mandatory validation gate and periodic role re-checks, not just a patch

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Prioritizes containment before full root-cause investigation
Methodically checks the documented RLS failure modes (role level, UPN format, model-wide scope)
Describes honest, timely stakeholder communication during the incident
Proposes a concrete post-incident process fix, not just a one-time patch

questions.title: SCD Type 2 at Scale: Surrogate Keys and the Rapidly-Changing Dimension Trap
questions.prompt: You're architecting the vendor dimension for an enterprise procurement warehouse. CreditRating and PreferredVendorStatus need full history. A junior engineer proposes versioning DimVendor keyed only on the natural key VendorID (no surrogate key), and a stakeholder separately wants CreditRating refreshed every single overnight batch because the vendor's credit score feed changes it almost daily. Write the real UPDATE+INSERT pattern for one Type 2 change on DimVendor, then explain in writing why dropping the surrogate key breaks this design at enterprise scale, and what you'd actually do about an attribute that changes too fast for Type 2 to stay sane.
questions.modelAnswer: Type 2 tracking requires a warehouse-generated surrogate key because the natural key (VendorID) is, by design, duplicated across every version of that vendor once history starts accumulating. If DimVendor were keyed only on VendorID, you could not have two rows for the same vendor at all — the primary key constraint forbids it — so there would be nothing to version onto in the first place. Fact rows also need to point at a specific point-in-time version of the vendor, not just 'this vendor in general'; a fact loaded last March has to keep pointing at the March version even after six more Type 2 changes happen. Only a surrogate key, incremented fresh on every version, gives you that stable, immutable join target. The correct pattern for one change is an UPDATE that closes the current row followed by an INSERT that opens the new version, run as a single transaction so a mid-failure never leaves the dimension with either two 'current' rows or zero: UPDATE to close the old row, then INSERT the new row with a fresh surrogate key, the same VendorID, the changed attribute value, and IsCurrent reset to 1. On the rapidly-changing attribute: if CreditRating is updated nightly and genuinely needs that cadence, full Type 2 versioning of it will explode row counts — a single vendor could accumulate hundreds of 'versions' a year, almost all differing by nothing but a credit score nobody is doing point-in-time analysis against. The fix is to pull CreditRating out of Type 2 tracking for DimVendor and either Type-1 overwrite it (if no report needs the historical value at all) or, if the business genuinely needs a time series of credit scores, move it into its own fact table (a 'vendor credit score snapshot' fact, one row per vendor per date) rather than versioning the whole vendor dimension around it. PreferredVendorStatus, which changes rarely and materially affects how historical purchase orders should be evaluated, stays Type 2 on DimVendor exactly as designed.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd push back on both proposals in the design review, for related reasons. First, no surrogate key: that's not a minor omission, it's a correctness bug waiting to happen, because the whole point of Type 2 is having two rows for the same vendor coexist, and a natural-key-only primary key makes that structurally impossible. I'd show them the UPDATE-then-INSERT pattern — close the old row's ExpirationDate and flip IsCurrent to 0, then insert a new row with a new identity surrogate key, same VendorID, the new attribute value, and IsCurrent back to 1 — wrapped in one transaction so we never get caught mid-change with either two current rows or none. On the nightly CreditRating refresh: I'd ask the stakeholder what they actually need — if nobody's ever going to ask 'what was this vendor's credit rating on the date of this specific PO,' then versioning it is pure overhead, and I'd just Type-1 overwrite it. If they do need a real time series, I wouldn't try to force that cadence into DimVendor's Type 2 columns at all — I'd split it into its own snapshot fact table, one row per vendor per day, and leave DimVendor's Type 2 tracking for the attributes that actually change at a human pace, like preferred-vendor status.
questions.example:
-- Single Type 2 change, closing the old version and opening the new one
BEGIN TRANSACTION;

UPDATE dw.DimVendor
SET    ExpirationDate = '2026-03-15',
       IsCurrent      = 0
WHERE  VendorKey = 4821
  AND  IsCurrent = 1;

INSERT INTO dw.DimVendor
    (VendorAlternateKey, VendorName, AccountNumber, CreditRating,
     PreferredVendorStatus, EffectiveDate, ExpirationDate, IsCurrent)
SELECT VendorAlternateKey, VendorName, AccountNumber, CreditRating,
       1 AS PreferredVendorStatus,          -- the attribute that changed
       '2026-03-15', '9999-12-31', 1
FROM   dw.DimVendor
WHERE  VendorKey = 4821 AND IsCurrent = 0;  -- carry forward unchanged columns

COMMIT TRANSACTION;
commonMistakes: Treats the surrogate key as optional boilerplate rather than the mechanism that makes Type 2 possible at all
Runs the UPDATE and INSERT as two separate statements with no transaction, risking a half-applied change
Applies Type 2 uniformly to every attribute on the dimension instead of classifying each one individually
Doesn't recognize a rapidly-changing attribute as a design smell and just lets version counts balloon
Fixes a rapidly-changing attribute by polling it less often instead of reconsidering whether it belongs in Type 2 at all
keyPoints: Explains why Type 2 is structurally impossible without a surrogate key
Names the UPDATE-then-INSERT pattern and wraps it in one transaction
Identifies rapidly-changing dimension as the real problem with the nightly CreditRating ask
Proposes a concrete alternative: Type 1 overwrite or a separate snapshot fact, not forcing Type 2 to cope
Keeps the hybrid classification attribute-by-attribute rather than all-or-nothing for the dimension

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct, transactional SCD Type 2 SQL pattern
Explains why surrogate key is structurally required
Correctly diagnoses rapidly-changing dimension risk
Proposes a concrete, workable alternative design

questions.title: Hybrid SCD Design for an Enterprise Customer Dimension
questions.prompt: A newly merged enterprise customer dimension carries: DateFirstPurchase, EmailAddress, PhoneNumber, CustomerSegment, MailingRegion, and PreferredContactMethod. The data governance team wants a single written policy — not a one-off decision — for how your team classifies SCD type on every future attribute added to this dimension, because three different teams have been guessing independently and producing inconsistent designs. Write that policy, apply it to classify all six attributes above with a one-line justification each, and explain what breaks in a mature warehouse if a team defaults to 'Type 2 everything' instead of following a real policy.
questions.modelAnswer: The policy is a single question, asked attribute by attribute, before any column is added to the dimension: does any report need this value exactly as it was at the time a related fact occurred? If no, and the change is a correction with no analytical value in the old value, classify it Type 1 (overwrite). If no, and the value is fixed by definition at insert time, classify it Type 0 (never changes). If yes, and the attribute materially affects historical rollups, classify it Type 2 (version it). If only the immediately prior value matters, not a full timeline, Type 3 applies, sparingly. Applied to the six attributes: DateFirstPurchase is Type 0 — it's fixed the moment it's recorded and is never really 'changed,' just set once. EmailAddress and PhoneNumber are Type 1 — these are operational contact corrections with no report depending on the historical value. CustomerSegment is Type 2 — 'revenue by segment, at the time of each order' requires the segment as it was then, not today, so overwriting it would silently rewrite history into every past rollup. MailingRegion is Type 2 for the identical reason — regional performance reporting needs the region that was true when each order shipped. PreferredContactMethod is Type 1 — it's purely operational, with no report depending on its history. A mature warehouse breaks in a specific way if a team defaults to 'Type 2 everything': every trivial correction — a typo fix in an email address, a formatting cleanup on a phone number — spawns a brand-new versioned row, and the dimension balloons with versions that carry no real analytical meaning. That bloat isn't just storage waste; it actively degrades query performance (more rows to scan and group), confuses analysts browsing the dimension (which version is 'the real one'?), and makes the ETL logic harder to reason about because every load has to guess which of dozens of near-identical versions is meaningful. The governance cost of a bad default compounds every time a new attribute gets added without going through the actual classification question.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd write this up as a one-page decision tree, not a long document, because the whole point is that three different teams can apply it independently and land on the same answer. The test is one question per attribute: does any report need this value exactly as it was at the time of a related fact? Walking the six: DateFirstPurchase is Type 0, it's set once and never really changes. Email and phone are Type 1 — nobody's running historical analysis against someone's old email address, those are just corrections. CustomerSegment and MailingRegion are both Type 2, and I'd be specific about why — if someone asks for 'revenue by segment last quarter,' that number has to reflect the segment each customer was actually in at the time, or the historical rollup silently rewrites itself every time a customer gets reclassified. PreferredContactMethod is Type 1, purely operational. On the 'Type 2 everything' failure mode — I've seen this in practice, and it's not a theoretical risk. A dimension where every typo fix spawns a new version balloons fast, and six months later analysts can't tell which of the fourteen rows for one customer is the one they actually want, and the ETL team is maintaining comparison logic against columns nobody needed versioned in the first place. The policy exists specifically so that doesn't happen by accident.
commonMistakes: Classifies attributes by 'how important does this feel' instead of the actual historical-need test
Defaults to Type 2 for everything as a false sense of safety, not realizing it has a real cost
Classifies DateFirstPurchase as Type 1 instead of recognizing it as fixed-at-insert (Type 0)
Misses that a hybrid dimension requires column-by-column ETL logic, not one comparison rule for the whole table
Treats the policy as a one-time decision instead of something applied to every future attribute added
keyPoints: States the single historical-need question as the actual decision rule
Correctly classifies all six attributes with a specific justification tied to a real report
Explains the concrete cost of defaulting to Type 2 everything, not just that it's 'wasteful'
Recognizes hybrid dimensions are the norm in mature warehouses, not an edge case
Frames the answer as a repeatable governance policy, not a one-off judgment call

evaluationCriteria.criterion: States a clear, repeatable classification rule
Correctly classifies all six attributes with justification
Explains the real cost of over-applying Type 2
Frames this as governance policy, not ad hoc judgment

questions.title: Choosing a Fact Table Type for a New Enterprise Process
questions.prompt: A new business process needs a fact table: a loan application that's submitted, then underwritten, then approved or denied, then funded — each stage recorded with its own date and some stages updating a running 'amount approved' figure on the same logical application. A junior data modeler on your team proposes a plain transaction fact table with one row inserted at each stage. Explain, as the architect reviewing this design, why that's the wrong classification, what the correct fact table type is, and walk through the grain, the milestone columns, and the measures the corrected design needs.
questions.modelAnswer: A plain transaction fact table captures an event once, at one immutable moment, and is never revisited — a single sale, a single scan. A loan application doesn't behave that way: it's opened once, and the same logical application progresses through milestones over time, with values like 'amount approved' updating in place as it moves. That lifecycle — one row, several milestone dates, measures that get revisited and updated rather than re-inserted at each stage — is the exact definition of an accumulating snapshot fact table, not a transaction fact. If the junior modeler's one-row-per-stage design ships, every report asking 'how many applications are currently at underwriting' or 'what's our average time from submission to funding' has to reconstruct the application's current state by finding the latest row per application and diffing timestamps — expensive, error-prone, and exactly the kind of logic an accumulating snapshot avoids by design. The corrected design: grain is one row per loan application. Milestone date keys: SubmittedDateKey, UnderwritingDateKey, DecisionDateKey, FundedDateKey — each nullable (or pointing at an 'unknown/not yet' DimDate row) until that stage actually happens, each updated in place as the application reaches that milestone, not inserted as a new row. Measures: RequestedAmount (set once at submission), ApprovedAmount (null until a decision is made, then updated), and optionally a duration measure like DaysToFund, computed once the final milestone lands. Degenerate dimension: the application number itself, riding directly on the fact row. The one tradeoff I'd flag back to the modeler: an accumulating snapshot needs UPDATE-capable ETL, not append-only inserts, which is a heavier load pattern than a transaction fact — but that's the correct cost for modeling a process with a real lifecycle instead of forcing it into a shape that doesn't match the business reality.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd stop this in design review before any DDL gets written, because the fact table type decision drives everything downstream. My first question back to the modeler would be: does this application get one immutable event, or does the same row change state over its life? It clearly changes state — submitted, underwritten, decided, funded — with an amount that gets filled in partway through. That's not a transaction fact, that's a textbook accumulating snapshot, and I'd point to the exact same shape we used on the work-order fact table in the capstone, where StockedQty and ScrappedQty updated in place as production progressed instead of a new row being inserted at every step. I'd walk the team through the corrected design live: grain is one row per application, four milestone date keys — submitted, underwriting, decision, funded — each one updated in place and nullable until that milestone actually happens, plus RequestedAmount and ApprovedAmount as measures that also update as the application moves. I'd be upfront about the tradeoff too: this means our load pattern needs UPDATE logic against existing rows, not just appends, which is more ETL complexity than a transaction fact needs — but forcing this into a one-row-per-event transaction fact would just push that same complexity onto every report instead of handling it once, correctly, in the warehouse.
commonMistakes: Classifies any multi-step business process as a transaction fact by default
Doesn't recognize 'values update in place over the row's life' as the defining signal for accumulating snapshot
Proposes one row per stage, forcing every downstream report to reconstruct current state manually
Forgets that milestone date columns need to be nullable until that milestone actually occurs
Fails to name the real tradeoff (update-heavy ETL) that comes with choosing accumulating snapshot
keyPoints: Correctly identifies the accumulating snapshot pattern from the lifecycle description
States the grain precisely as one row per application
Lists milestone date keys as nullable, update-in-place columns
Identifies measures that update over the row's life versus those set once
Names the real tradeoff: update-capable ETL instead of append-only loads

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly diagnoses accumulating snapshot vs transaction fact
Designs correct grain and milestone date columns
Designs correct measures, including update-in-place behavior
Names the real ETL tradeoff of this fact type

questions.title: Bridge Table Design for a Many-to-Many Sales Credit Relationship
questions.prompt: An enterprise sales organization splits credit for large deals across multiple salespeople, and a single salesperson is naturally credited on many deals — a genuine many-to-many relationship. Design the bridge table that resolves this against a Sale fact table and a Salesperson dimension: write the real DDL, explain why a bridge table with no other columns is itself a specific fact table type, and explain what goes wrong for a three-way-split deal if the team instead tries to force a single SalespersonKey foreign key directly onto the fact table.
questions.modelAnswer: A bridge table resolves a genuine many-to-many relationship by sitting between the fact and the dimension, storing one row per valid combination, turning one many-to-many relationship into two clean one-to-many relationships: the fact relates to the bridge table, and the bridge table relates to the dimension. For sales-credit splitting, the bridge table (SaleSalesperson) stores one row per (SaleID, SalespersonKey) pairing. If a deal is split three ways, the bridge table gets exactly three rows, each pointing at the same sale and a different salesperson. A bridge table containing nothing but foreign keys — no measures, no numeric columns to sum — is, by definition, a factless fact table: a row records that an association happened (this salesperson was credited on this sale), and the only thing you can measure from it is a count of rows, not a sum. If the team instead forces a single SalespersonKey directly onto the Sale fact table, a three-way-split deal has nowhere to put the second and third salesperson — the design can only represent one salesperson per sale row. The team is then forced into a bad compromise: either arbitrarily picking one salesperson per deal (which is simply wrong data, understating credit for the other two), or duplicating the entire fact row once per salesperson (which double- or triple-counts every measure on that row — revenue, quantity, everything — the instant someone runs a SUM without remembering to de-duplicate first). The bridge table avoids both failure modes: the Sale fact table keeps its true one-row-per-sale grain with correct, unduplicated measures, and credit-splitting is answered by joining through the bridge, with weighting (e.g., a SplitPercentage column added to the bridge table) handling partial credit cleanly if the business needs it.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd draw this on the whiteboard before writing any DDL, because the moment someone proposes a single SalespersonKey on the Sale fact, I want the room to see exactly where it breaks: a three-way split deal literally has no second or third slot to put the other two salespeople, so you either lie about credit or duplicate the whole row and blow up every measure the instant someone sums revenue without remembering to de-duplicate. The fix is a bridge table — one row per sale-salesperson pair, nothing but foreign keys, which makes it a factless fact table by definition, countable but not summable on its own. I'd add a SplitPercentage column from day one even if nobody's asked for partial credit yet, because 'three people split this deal evenly' is rarely how real sales credit actually works, and retrofitting a weighting column later always costs more than building it in now. The fact table keeps its clean one-row-per-sale grain, the bridge handles the many-to-many, and nobody's measures get silently inflated.
questions.example:
-- Bridge table: resolves many-to-many sale-to-salesperson credit
CREATE TABLE dw.BridgeSaleSalesperson (
    SaleID           BIGINT        NOT NULL REFERENCES dw.FactSale(SaleID),
    SalespersonKey   INT           NOT NULL REFERENCES dw.DimSalesperson(SalespersonKey),
    SplitPercentage  DECIMAL(5,2)  NOT NULL DEFAULT 100.00,  -- optional: partial credit
    CONSTRAINT PK_BridgeSaleSalesperson PRIMARY KEY (SaleID, SalespersonKey)
);

-- A sale split three ways produces three bridge rows
INSERT INTO dw.BridgeSaleSalesperson (SaleID, SalespersonKey, SplitPercentage)
VALUES (90214, 101, 40.00),
       (90214, 118, 35.00),
       (90214, 203, 25.00);

-- Credited revenue per salesperson, correctly weighted, no fact-row duplication
SELECT b.SalespersonKey,
       SUM(f.SalesAmount * b.SplitPercentage / 100.0) AS CreditedRevenue
FROM   dw.FactSale f
JOIN   dw.BridgeSaleSalesperson b ON f.SaleID = b.SaleID
GROUP BY b.SalespersonKey;
commonMistakes: Forces a single FK onto the fact table and arbitrarily picks one salesperson per deal
Duplicates the fact row per salesperson, double-counting every measure on a GROUP BY SUM
Doesn't recognize a columns-only bridge table as a factless fact table
Forgets a composite primary key on the bridge table, allowing duplicate credit rows
Omits a weighting column when the business genuinely needs partial, not equal, credit

Writes a working bridge table DDL with a correct composite key
Explains why a columns-only bridge table is a factless fact table
Explains the double-counting failure mode of forcing a single FK instead
Shows how to query through the bridge table without duplicating measures
