questions.title: Columnstore Indexing Strategy Across a Multi-Billion-Row Warehouse
questions.prompt: Your enterprise warehouse has a mix of fact tables: a 4-billion-row sales fact that's purely analytical, and a 200-million-row order fact that operational staff also query one order at a time by order number for customer service lookups. The DBA team's default policy is 'clustered columnstore on every fact table, no exceptions.' As the architect, decide the indexing strategy for both tables and justify any deviation from the blanket policy — including what you'd tell the DBA team about why 'no exceptions' is the wrong policy here.
questions.modelAnswer: For the 4-billion-row sales fact, a clustered columnstore index is correct and should be the default without exception: it's scanned and aggregated across huge row counts, and a traditional rowstore B-tree index would force SQL Server to visit and decompress full rows for every column touched by an aggregate — exactly the workload columnstore's column-by-column compressed storage and batch-mode execution is built for. For the 200-million-row order fact, the blanket policy breaks down because the workload isn't purely analytical: operational staff doing single-order lookups by order number need fast point lookups, which a clustered columnstore index does not serve well — it has no efficient single-row seek path the way a rowstore B-tree does. Converting that table fully to columnstore would make the customer-service lookup path slow, trading one workload's performance for the other's. The correct design keeps the order fact as a normal rowstore table, with its usual clustered rowstore index supporting the order-number lookup, and adds a nonclustered columnstore index covering just the analytical columns (dates, amounts, dimension keys) that reporting actually aggregates over. This gives analytical queries the columnar, batch-mode performance benefit on the columns that matter for reporting, while the operational lookup path keeps its fast row-by-row access unchanged. What I'd tell the DBA team: 'clustered columnstore by default' is the right instinct for fact tables in general, but a blanket no-exceptions policy conflates 'this table is large' with 'this table's access pattern is purely analytical' — and those aren't the same thing. The real decision criterion isn't row count, it's whether the table has a genuine mixed workload, and the order fact clearly does.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd tell the DBA team the policy is right for the sales fact and wrong, as written, for the order fact — and I'd be specific about why rather than just overruling it. The sales fact is a pure analytical workload at huge scale, so clustered columnstore is exactly the textbook case: it's scanned and summed, not looked up row by row, and columnstore's compression and batch-mode execution is built for that. The order fact is different in a way that matters — customer service is doing single-order lookups by order number all day, and a clustered columnstore table has no fast seek path for that; converting it fully to columnstore would quietly tank that operational workload to speed up analytics that honestly don't need it that badly at 200 million rows. I'd keep the order fact as rowstore with its normal clustered index on order number, and add a nonclustered columnstore index over just the analytical columns — dates, amounts, the dimension keys — so reporting still gets the columnar benefit where it matters without breaking the lookup path. The policy I'd actually propose back to the DBA team isn't 'no exceptions,' it's 'default to clustered columnstore unless the table has a genuine mixed read pattern, and here's the one table in our estate that does.'
commonMistakes: Applies 'bigger table, more columnstore' as the decision rule instead of looking at the actual access pattern
Converts a mixed-workload table fully to columnstore and silently breaks operational lookups
Doesn't know nonclustered columnstore exists as a middle option alongside a still-rowstore table
Treats the DBA team's blanket policy as something to simply override rather than explain
Fails to name row-count scale as a legitimate but insufficient justification on its own
keyPoints: Correctly applies clustered columnstore to the purely analytical fact table
Identifies the order fact's mixed workload as the reason to deviate
Proposes nonclustered columnstore as the concrete middle-ground solution
Articulates the real decision criterion (workload shape, not row count) back to the DBA team
Frames the deviation as a justified exception, not a rejection of the whole policy

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct indexing decision for the pure-analytical fact table
Correctly identifies mixed workload and deviates appropriately
Proposes a concrete, working nonclustered columnstore solution
Articulates the right general decision criterion to the DBA team

questions.title: Writing the Type 2 Load Pattern for a Vendor Status Change
questions.prompt: Vendor 758596752 (surrogate key 296, currently IsCurrent = 1) moves from CreditRating 3 to CreditRating 5 and PreferredVendorStatus flips from 0 to 1, effective 2026-02-01. DimVendor is Type 2 on both attributes. Write the exact SQL you'd run — as a single unit of work — to close out the old version and insert the new one, carrying forward every unchanged column correctly, and add the one safeguard that stops this exact script from silently corrupting the dimension if it's accidentally run twice.
questions.modelAnswer: The load has three real requirements: close the old row, insert a correctly-populated new row carrying forward unchanged attributes, and do both as one transaction so a mid-failure never leaves two current rows or zero current rows for this vendor. The safeguard against a double-run is an idempotency check: before doing anything, verify there isn't already a current row for this vendor with the new attribute values already in place — if the script is re-run, it should detect that the intended change already happened and do nothing, rather than closing an already-closed row (a no-op that's harmless) or, worse, inserting a second duplicate 'new' version (which is the actual corruption risk — two IsCurrent=1 rows for the same vendor breaks every downstream join). The safest implementation guards the INSERT with a condition checking the current row's values don't already match the incoming change, inside the same transaction as the UPDATE, so the whole operation is naturally idempotent.
questions.professionalAnswer: Two things I'd insist on before this script goes anywhere near a scheduled job: it runs as one transaction, and it's safe to run twice. The transaction part is obvious once you say it out loud — if the UPDATE commits and the INSERT fails, this vendor now has zero current rows, and every fact load after that point fails its dimension lookup. The idempotency part is the one people skip, and it's the one that actually bites in production, because retries happen — a job gets kicked off twice, a network blip causes a re-run, whatever. So before I touch anything, I check whether the current row already reflects the change I'm about to make; if it does, I do nothing. That one guard is the difference between a script that's safe to re-run and one that quietly doubles up current rows the second time ops accidentally fires it.
questions.example:
BEGIN TRANSACTION;

-- Idempotency guard: only proceed if the current row doesn't already reflect this change
IF EXISTS (
    SELECT 1 FROM dw.DimVendor
    WHERE VendorKey = 296 AND IsCurrent = 1
      AND NOT (CreditRating = 5 AND PreferredVendorStatus = 1)
)
BEGIN
    UPDATE dw.DimVendor
    SET    ExpirationDate = '2026-02-01',
           IsCurrent      = 0
    WHERE  VendorKey = 296
      AND  IsCurrent = 1;

    INSERT INTO dw.DimVendor
        (VendorAlternateKey, VendorName, AccountNumber,
         CreditRating, PreferredVendorStatus,
         EffectiveDate, ExpirationDate, IsCurrent)
    SELECT VendorAlternateKey, VendorName, AccountNumber,
           5, 1,                       -- the changed attributes
           '2026-02-01', '9999-12-31', 1
    FROM   dw.DimVendor
    WHERE  VendorKey = 296 AND IsCurrent = 0
      AND  ExpirationDate = '2026-02-01';  -- the row we just closed
END

COMMIT TRANSACTION;
commonMistakes: Runs the UPDATE and INSERT as separate statements with no transaction
Hardcodes the carried-forward attribute values instead of selecting them from the existing row
Has no idempotency guard, so a retried or duplicated job run inserts a second current row
Forgets to filter the UPDATE's WHERE clause to IsCurrent = 1, risking closing the wrong row
Leaves ExpirationDate off the new row or sets it to NULL instead of a far-future sentinel date
keyPoints: Correct UPDATE-then-INSERT sequence wrapped in one transaction
New row correctly carries forward unchanged attribute values from the old row
Explicit idempotency guard prevents duplicate current rows on a re-run
WHERE clauses correctly scoped to IsCurrent = 1 before the change
New row's ExpirationDate set to a proper far-future sentinel, not NULL

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct, transactional UPDATE+INSERT SQL
Correctly carries forward unchanged attributes
Working idempotency safeguard against double-run
Correct WHERE scoping and sentinel date handling

questions.title: Partitioned, Columnstore-Indexed Fact Table for a High-Volume Warehouse
questions.prompt: You're standing up FactPurchaseOrderLine for an enterprise procurement warehouse expected to grow past 2 billion rows within three years, with a 7-year retention policy and nightly purges of data past that window. Write the complete physical design: the CREATE TABLE with correct data types and keys, the partition function and scheme keyed on order date, and the columnstore indexing decision — and explain specifically how your partitioning choice makes the nightly retention purge fast instead of a slow row-by-row DELETE.
questions.modelAnswer: The physical design needs four pieces working together: correct warehouse-style data types (INT YYYYMMDD date keys, DECIMAL/MONEY measures, surrogate FKs), a partition function and scheme keyed on the date column so each year's (or quarter's) data lives in its own physical partition, the table created ON that scheme rather than on a single filegroup, and a clustered columnstore index for analytical scan performance. The retention purge is fast specifically because of partitioning: ALTER TABLE ... SWITCH PARTITION moves an entire partition out of the table as a near-instant metadata operation, regardless of how many rows that partition holds — no row-by-row logged DELETE at all. For a 7-year retention policy, the purge job identifies the partition holding data older than 7 years, switches it into a staging table (or drops it directly if no archival is needed), and the main fact table instantly has 7 years and one day's less data with none of the I/O or transaction-log cost a billion-row DELETE would incur. This only works because the partitioning column (OrderDateKey) is also the retention boundary column — if they didn't line up, SWITCH couldn't cleanly isolate 'everything older than 7 years' into one or a few partitions.
questions.professionalAnswer: At 2 billion rows I treat partitioning and columnstore as two separate decisions that both have to be right, not one bundled choice. Columnstore gets me fast aggregate scans; partitioning gets me fast data lifecycle management, and the second one is what actually makes the 7-year retention policy tractable. The detail I always flag to the team: your partitioning column has to be the same column your retention policy keys off of, which here is the order date, because SWITCH PARTITION is a metadata operation — it reassigns a partition's pages instantly, it doesn't walk rows — but only if what you want to remove maps cleanly onto one or a few whole partitions. If you partition on something else and retention is keyed on date, you're back to a billion-row logged DELETE every purge cycle, which defeats the entire point. I'd also size the surrogate key as BIGINT up front — INT caps out well under where this table is headed in three years, and that's a painful migration to do later on a live, partitioned, columnstore-indexed table.
questions.example:
-- Partition function: yearly boundaries on an INT YYYYMMDD date key
CREATE PARTITION FUNCTION PF_FactPOLine_ByYear (INT)
    AS RANGE RIGHT FOR VALUES (20210101, 20220101, 20230101, 20240101, 20250101, 20260101);

CREATE PARTITION SCHEME PS_FactPOLine_ByYear
    AS PARTITION PF_FactPOLine_ByYear ALL TO ([PRIMARY]);

CREATE TABLE dw.FactPurchaseOrderLine (
    PurchaseOrderLineKey BIGINT       NOT NULL,   -- BIGINT: table will exceed 2B rows
    VendorKey       INT           NOT NULL,
    ProductKey      INT           NOT NULL,
    OrderDateKey    INT           NOT NULL,       -- partitioning + retention column
    DueDateKey      INT           NULL,
    ShipDateKey     INT           NULL,
    PurchaseOrderID INT           NOT NULL,
    OrderQty        SMALLINT      NOT NULL,
    UnitPrice       DECIMAL(19,4) NOT NULL,
    LineTotal       DECIMAL(19,4) NOT NULL,
    ReceivedQty     DECIMAL(9,2)  NOT NULL DEFAULT 0
) ON PS_FactPOLine_ByYear (OrderDateKey);

-- Clustered columnstore for analytical scans, built on the partitioned table
CREATE CLUSTERED COLUMNSTORE INDEX CCI_FactPurchaseOrderLine
    ON dw.FactPurchaseOrderLine;

-- Nightly retention purge: switch the oldest partition out instead of DELETE
ALTER TABLE dw.FactPurchaseOrderLine
    SWITCH PARTITION 1 TO dw.FactPurchaseOrderLine_Archive PARTITION 1;
commonMistakes: Uses INT instead of BIGINT for the surrogate key on a table sized to exceed 2 billion rows
Creates the partition function/scheme but forgets to create the table ON that scheme
Picks a partitioning column that doesn't match the retention policy's boundary, breaking fast SWITCH purges
Tries to combine partitioning with a row-by-row DELETE instead of using SWITCH PARTITION
Forgets the clustered columnstore index entirely, leaving the table as a slow rowstore heap
keyPoints: Correct data types sized for the table's real scale (BIGINT surrogate key)
Partition function and scheme correctly keyed on the date column
Table created ON the partition scheme, not a single filegroup
Clustered columnstore index applied for analytical scan performance
Explains SWITCH PARTITION as a metadata-only operation that makes retention purges fast

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct, complete CREATE TABLE with appropriate data types
Correct partition function/scheme keyed on the right column
Correct columnstore indexing decision
Explains why SWITCH PARTITION makes retention purges fast

questions.title: Writing an Enterprise-Scale Staging Validation Suite
questions.prompt: A new source feed is being onboarded into staging for an enterprise order warehouse: stg.OrderLine, which should have no nulls in CustomerID or ProductID, every ProductID present in dw.DimProduct, no duplicate (OrderID, OrderLineID) pairs, and no negative LineTotal values. Write the four validation queries, one per category, that a staging QA process should run before this data is allowed into the warehouse, and explain which specific response — reject and log, default and flag, or fail the whole batch — you'd apply to each category's failures and why.
questions.modelAnswer: Each of the four categories gets its own check, and the response policy differs by category because the categories carry different risk. Nulls in required fields (CustomerID, ProductID): reject and log to a quarantine table — these rows can't be safely defaulted without fabricating a customer or product, and loading them with a placeholder key would silently corrupt customer- or product-level rollups. Referential integrity (ProductID missing from DimProduct): default and flag to an 'Unknown Product' member row with IsInferredMember-style tracking, rather than rejecting outright, because the order genuinely happened and excluding it would understate real sales volume — but it must be flagged so it's traceable and correctable once the real product dimension catches up. Duplicates on (OrderID, OrderLineID): reject and log the extra copies — a duplicate is never correct data, it's a re-run or an upstream resend, and silently summing it would double-count revenue. Negative LineTotal: this is severe enough to consider failing the whole batch if the count is high relative to normal volume (suggesting an upstream currency or sign-flip bug), but for a small number of isolated rows, reject and log is the proportionate response — either way, a negative line total should never silently load as-is into a fact table measure.
questions.professionalAnswer: I don't apply one blanket policy to every failed row — I ask what each category of failure actually means for the business before deciding what to do with it. A null CustomerID or ProductID, I reject and quarantine, full stop, because I can't fabricate an identity for either without corrupting a rollup somewhere. An orphaned ProductID is different — the order really happened, the sale is real, so excluding it just makes our revenue number quietly wrong in the other direction. I'd rather default it to an Unknown Product member, flag it so it's traceable, and reconcile it once the real product dimension catches up. Duplicates I always reject outright — there's no version of 'keep the duplicate' that doesn't double-count revenue. And negative LineTotal is where I draw a volume-based line: a couple of isolated rows, quarantine and move on; a sudden spike in negative values, that's not a data-quality blip, that's probably an upstream sign-flip or currency bug, and I'd rather fail the whole batch and investigate than load a systematically wrong number into the warehouse.
questions.example:
-- 1. Nulls in required fields
SELECT * FROM stg.OrderLine
WHERE CustomerID IS NULL OR ProductID IS NULL;

-- 2. Referential integrity: ProductID missing from DimProduct
SELECT s.*
FROM   stg.OrderLine s
LEFT JOIN dw.DimProduct p ON s.ProductID = p.ProductAlternateKey
WHERE  p.ProductAlternateKey IS NULL;

-- 3. Duplicates on the natural key
SELECT OrderID, OrderLineID, COUNT(*) AS DupeCount
FROM   stg.OrderLine
GROUP BY OrderID, OrderLineID
HAVING COUNT(*) > 1;

-- 4. Type/format: LineTotal fails to be a valid, non-negative number
SELECT * FROM stg.OrderLine
WHERE TRY_CONVERT(DECIMAL(19,4), LineTotal) IS NULL
   OR TRY_CONVERT(DECIMAL(19,4), LineTotal) < 0;
commonMistakes: Writes one generic validation query instead of one per distinct check category
Applies the same response (always reject, or always default) to every category regardless of risk
Rejects orphaned ProductID rows outright instead of considering default-and-flag to avoid understating volume
Doesn't flag defaulted rows, making them untraceable once the real data arrives
Uses a plain CAST instead of TRY_CONVERT, which errors the whole query on one bad value instead of flagging it
keyPoints: Writes four correct, distinct validation queries, one per category
Assigns a deliberate, differentiated response policy per category rather than one blanket rule
Recognizes that referential-integrity failures may deserve default-and-flag rather than rejection
Recognizes duplicates should always be rejected, never summed
Ties the fail-the-batch option to a volume threshold, not a single bad row

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Four correct, working validation queries
Differentiated, justified response policy per category
Correct handling of type/format validation without erroring
Recognizes quarantine/traceability as non-negotiable

questions.title: Building and Maintaining an Aggregate Table at Enterprise Scale
questions.prompt: A 500-million-row FactSale table is bottlenecking the executive revenue dashboard, which only ever asks for revenue by month and region. Write the CTAS statement that builds an aggregate table solving this, write the refresh procedure that keeps it in sync after each nightly load, and explain the one failure mode that makes aggregate tables risky at enterprise scale if ownership of the refresh schedule isn't explicit.
questions.modelAnswer: An aggregate fact table rolls the detailed fact up to a coarser grain the common queries actually need — here, month and region instead of individual sale lines — built with CTAS and refreshed on a schedule as part of the warehouse's regular ETL orchestration, not as a one-off query. The refresh has to run after the detailed fact table's own nightly load completes, in dependency order, exactly like a dimension-before-fact ordering rule. The real enterprise-scale risk isn't the CTAS itself — it's that an aggregate table is a deliberate duplication of data, and duplication only stays correct if its refresh is treated as a first-class, monitored step in the pipeline. If ownership of that refresh schedule isn't explicit — if it's a stored procedure nobody put in the job dependency chain, or a job that silently stops firing after a server migration — the aggregate table drifts out of sync with the detail, and the executive dashboard starts confidently reporting a stale number that disagrees with the detailed fact table underneath it. That's strictly worse than the original slow-query problem, because a slow query is visibly slow, while a stale aggregate looks completely normal until someone cross-checks it against the detail and finds a mismatch. The mitigation is to make the aggregate refresh a scheduled, monitored step with the same failure alerting as the rest of the pipeline, and to add a periodic reconciliation check comparing aggregate totals against the detail.
questions.professionalAnswer: The CTAS itself is the easy five minutes of this problem. What I actually care about when I propose an aggregate table is who owns its refresh and whether that refresh is wired into the same dependency chain as everything else. An aggregate table is duplicated data by design, and duplicated data that silently falls out of sync is worse than the slow query it replaced, because a slow query tells you something's wrong immediately, and a stale aggregate just sits there looking correct until an exec cross-checks it against the detail in a meeting and asks why the numbers don't match. So I always build the refresh as a scheduled step that fails loudly and gets monitored like every other job in the pipeline, sequenced after the detail fact load, never as a stored procedure someone remembers to run by hand. And I'd add one more thing most people skip — a periodic reconciliation check that just compares the aggregate's totals against the detail and alerts if they drift, because that's the cheapest insurance against the exact failure mode that makes aggregate tables risky at scale.
questions.example:
-- Build the aggregate table once
CREATE TABLE dw.Agg_Sale_ByMonth_Region AS
SELECT d.CalendarYear, d.MonthNumberOfYear, r.Region,
       SUM(f.SalesAmount) AS TotalRevenue,
       COUNT(*) AS LineCount
FROM   dw.FactSale f
JOIN   dw.DimDate d   ON f.OrderDateKey = d.DateKey
JOIN   dw.DimRegion r ON f.RegionKey = r.RegionKey
GROUP BY d.CalendarYear, d.MonthNumberOfYear, r.Region;

-- Nightly refresh procedure, run AFTER the detailed fact load completes
CREATE OR ALTER PROCEDURE dw.Refresh_Agg_Sale_ByMonth_Region
AS
BEGIN
    TRUNCATE TABLE dw.Agg_Sale_ByMonth_Region;

    INSERT INTO dw.Agg_Sale_ByMonth_Region
    SELECT d.CalendarYear, d.MonthNumberOfYear, r.Region,
           SUM(f.SalesAmount), COUNT(*)
    FROM   dw.FactSale f
    JOIN   dw.DimDate d   ON f.OrderDateKey = d.DateKey
    JOIN   dw.DimRegion r ON f.RegionKey = r.RegionKey
    GROUP BY d.CalendarYear, d.MonthNumberOfYear, r.Region;
END;
commonMistakes: Treats the CTAS as a one-off query instead of wiring it into scheduled, monitored ETL orchestration
Doesn't sequence the aggregate refresh after the detailed fact load, risking a stale or half-loaded aggregate
Assumes an aggregate table is a free performance win with no ongoing maintenance cost
Fails to name the real enterprise risk: silent staleness going unnoticed versus an obviously-slow query
Doesn't propose any reconciliation check between the aggregate and the detail
keyPoints: Correct CTAS building the aggregate at the right grain
Correct refresh procedure sequenced after the detailed fact load
Identifies silent staleness, not query cost, as the real enterprise-scale risk
Proposes explicit ownership/monitoring of the refresh schedule as the mitigation
Mentions reconciliation checks against the detail table

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct CTAS at the right grain
Correct, properly sequenced refresh procedure
Correctly identifies the silent-staleness risk at scale
Proposes a concrete mitigation (monitoring/reconciliation)

questions.title: Writing the Inferred-Member Pattern for a Late-Arriving Customer
questions.prompt: A loyalty membership fact needs to load the instant a new member's first transaction happens, but the member's real name, address, and segment details arrive through a separate onboarding feed, sometimes days later. Write the fact-load logic that handles a failed DimCustomer lookup by inserting an inferred member row, and separately write the update that resolves that inferred row once the real details arrive — and explain, precisely, why that second update must not be implemented as an SCD Type 2 change.
questions.modelAnswer: When the fact load process looks up a dimension key and the lookup fails but the natural key is trusted (a real loyalty number was issued), the correct response is to insert a new dimension row immediately, using placeholder 'Unknown' values for every attribute except the natural key, and set an audit attribute, IsInferredMember, to TRUE. This lets the fact row load now, with a valid surrogate key, instead of being blocked or falling back to a generic 'Unknown Customer' row that would lose the ability to ever connect this fact to the real customer later. When the real onboarding details arrive, the correct handling is to update the existing inferred row's attributes in place and flip IsInferredMember to FALSE — not to run it through SCD Type 2 logic. The reason is structural: an SCD Type 2 change exists to preserve a 'before' state that was once true and worth keeping for historical reporting. An inferred row never had a real 'before' state — its placeholder values were never true at any point in time, they were just a stand-in for missing information. Versioning it with Type 2 would create a permanent historical row representing a value that was never actually real, polluting the dimension's history with a fabricated 'first version' that no fact should ever be interpreted as referring to. Updating in place is correct precisely because there's nothing legitimate to preserve.
questions.professionalAnswer: The key design decision here is what happens on a failed lookup, and I always push back on routing it to a generic Unknown row, because that throws away the one piece of information we actually have — the real loyalty number. Instead I insert a proper dimension row keyed on that real natural key, fill everything else with Unknown placeholders, and flag it IsInferredMember so it's traceable. The part people get wrong is what happens when the real details show up later — I've seen engineers reach for SCD Type 2 instinctively because 'the data changed,' but Type 2 exists to preserve a before-state that was actually true at some point, and an inferred row's placeholder values were never true, they were just a gap-filler. There's nothing worth versioning. So that update is a plain in-place UPDATE, flip the flag to false, done — treating it as late-arriving detail, not a slowly changing dimension event.
questions.example:
-- Fact load: dimension lookup fails but the natural key (loyalty number) is trusted
IF NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM dw.DimCustomer WHERE CustomerAlternateKey = @LoyaltyNumber)
BEGIN
    INSERT INTO dw.DimCustomer
        (CustomerAlternateKey, FullName, Address, Segment, IsInferredMember)
    VALUES
        (@LoyaltyNumber, 'Unknown', 'Unknown', 'Unknown', 1);
END

-- Later: real onboarding details arrive. Update in place, NOT a Type 2 version.
UPDATE dw.DimCustomer
SET    FullName          = @RealFullName,
       Address            = @RealAddress,
       Segment            = @RealSegment,
       IsInferredMember   = 0
WHERE  CustomerAlternateKey = @LoyaltyNumber
  AND  IsInferredMember = 1;
commonMistakes: Falls back to a generic 'Unknown Customer' row instead of inserting a new inferred member tied to the real natural key
Forgets to set IsInferredMember = TRUE on the newly inserted row, losing track of which rows need resolution
Implements the later update as an SCD Type 2 change, creating a fake historical 'version' that was never true
Doesn't flip IsInferredMember back to FALSE once real details are applied
Blocks the fact load entirely while waiting for the dimension lookup to succeed
keyPoints: Correctly inserts an inferred member row with placeholder values on a failed lookup, keyed to the real natural key
Correctly sets and later clears the IsInferredMember audit flag
Explains precisely why there's no legitimate 'before' state to preserve, ruling out Type 2
Keeps the resolution as a plain in-place UPDATE
Recognizes this as late-arriving dimension detail handling, distinct from SCD logic

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct inferred-member insert logic on failed lookup
Correct in-place update resolving the inferred row later
Precise explanation of why this isn't an SCD Type 2 change
Correct IsInferredMember flag handling throughout

questions.title: Root-Causing Eight Months of Corrupted Fact-Table Foreign Keys
questions.prompt: A late-arriving-dimension bug has been silently corrupting fact-table foreign keys for eight months: a dimension-key lookup failure was falling back to a generic 'Unknown Member' row (surrogate key 0) instead of creating a proper inferred member, so thousands of facts across that whole period point at the same meaningless placeholder row instead of their real, now-identifiable dimension members. Walk through how you diagnose this as the root cause (not just the symptom), the fix for the load logic going forward, and how you'd actually repair the eight months of already-corrupted fact rows without re-running the entire historical load.
questions.modelAnswer: The symptom is almost certainly first noticed as a report anomaly — an oddly large volume of activity attributed to 'Unknown' in a dimension slice, or a rollup where a known member's numbers look lower than expected because their real activity is hiding under surrogate key 0. Diagnosing the root cause, not just patching the report, means tracing backward through the ETL: check whether the fact load's dimension-key lookup has a fallback branch, and specifically whether that fallback routes to a generic Unknown row versus inserting a proper inferred member with the real natural key preserved. If it routes to a generic Unknown row, the fix is structural: replace that fallback with the inferred-member pattern — insert a new dimension row keyed on the real natural key with placeholder attributes and IsInferredMember = TRUE, so future lookup failures are tied to an identifiable row instead of being anonymized into one meaningless bucket. Repairing eight months of already-corrupted history without a full re-run requires reconstructing, after the fact, which Unknown-keyed fact rows actually belonged to which real natural key — this only works if the natural key (or some other identifying attribute) survived on the fact row itself, even though the dimension key didn't resolve correctly. If the fact table retained a degenerate attribute or source system ID that identifies the real entity, the repair is a targeted UPDATE: for each real natural key that should have had an inferred member, insert the correct dimension row now, then UPDATE only the affected fact rows (filtered to the surrogate key 0 placeholder, joined back to source data by natural key) to point at the correct new dimension key instead. If no identifying attribute survived on the fact row at all, this is the harder case — the fix may require re-extracting from the original source system's historical data (if retained) rather than the warehouse's own already-corrupted copy, since the information needed to repair it was lost at load time, not just misrouted.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd start by refusing to treat this as 'the report is wrong, let's fix the report' — that's treating a data-corruption problem as a presentation problem, and it'll just resurface somewhere else. I'd trace the actual ETL logic for the dimension lookup and confirm my suspicion: somewhere, a failed lookup is falling back to a shared 'Unknown' row instead of creating a proper inferred member tied to the real natural key. Once that's confirmed, the forward fix is straightforward — swap that fallback for the inferred-member pattern so every future lookup failure at least preserves the real identity, flagged for later resolution. The harder conversation is about the eight months already in production. I would not propose re-running the entire historical load — that's a blunt, expensive, and risky instrument for a targeted problem. Instead I'd check whether the fact rows retained any identifying detail — a source system ID, a degenerate dimension column — that survived even though the dimension key resolution didn't. If it did, I can reconstruct the correct mapping and run a scoped, auditable UPDATE against just the affected rows. If it didn't, I'd be honest with the team that this is a data-loss situation, not just a bug, and the real fix may require going back to the original source system's retained history rather than our own corrupted copy — and I'd flag that finding as the reason we need retention policy and audit columns reviewed, so this specific failure mode can't happen silently again.
commonMistakes: Treats this as a reporting bug and patches the report instead of the load logic
Proposes a full historical re-run as the default fix without checking if a targeted repair is possible
Doesn't check whether identifying information survived on the fact row before declaring the data unrecoverable
Fixes the forward-going load logic but doesn't address the already-corrupted eight months at all
Doesn't distinguish between a generic Unknown-row fallback and a proper inferred-member pattern as the actual root cause
keyPoints: Correctly identifies the generic-Unknown-row fallback as the structural root cause
Proposes the inferred-member pattern as the correct forward-going fix
Checks whether a targeted repair is possible before resorting to a full re-run
Explains the repair mechanics: reconstruct mapping, insert correct members, update affected rows
Is honest about the harder case where identifying information didn't survive

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly diagnoses the structural root cause, not just the symptom
Proposes the correct forward-going fix (inferred-member pattern)
Designs a targeted, auditable repair instead of defaulting to a full re-run
Acknowledges the harder data-loss case honestly

questions.title: Leading the Incident: Last Night's Load Doubled Revenue Before an Exec Presentation
questions.prompt: It's 7 AM. The executive team presents quarterly revenue to the board at 9 AM, and this morning's dashboard shows revenue roughly double what it should be. Your team believes last night's warehouse load is the cause but hasn't confirmed it. Walk through exactly how you run this incident in the two hours you have: what you check first, how you decide whether to fix it, roll it back, or pull the dashboard, and specifically what you tell the executive team and when.
questions.modelAnswer: With two hours and a board presentation at stake, the priority order is: stop the bleeding, confirm scope, decide on a safe state, then communicate — in that order, not communication first. First ten minutes: confirm the load actually ran and check row counts between the detailed fact table and its known-good source — a doubled revenue number is a classic symptom of a join fan-out (a lookup join that unintentionally matched more than one row) or an accidental double-insert from a re-run. Running the same row-count parity check used for validation (source count vs. staging count vs. fact count) immediately tells you whether rows were duplicated outright. Next 20 minutes: if the fact table's row count is roughly double what it should be for last night's load window specifically, that confirms a duplication bug scoped to last night's run, not a months-old issue — which matters because it tells you the historical numbers before last night are probably fine, only today's incremental load is suspect. Decision point at the 30-40 minute mark: the safest action, given the time pressure, is almost never 'patch the ETL logic live and re-run' — that's unverified under pressure and risks a second bad state. The safer options are to roll back last night's incremental load specifically (if the load pattern supports isolating and reversing just that batch) or to point the executive dashboard's data source at a known-good prior snapshot or the pre-refresh semantic model cache while the real fix gets properly tested. Communication to the executive team should happen as soon as the problem is confirmed and scoped — not before you're sure, and not after you've silently fixed it without telling them. The message is never 'the numbers are wrong, sorry' with no plan — it's 'we caught a data issue in last night's load, here's what's confirmed affected, here's the corrected number or the safe fallback we're presenting with instead, and here's when the permanent fix lands.' Mitigation comes before root-causing in the message, because executives walking into a board meeting need a number they can trust right now, not a postmortem.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd run this like any incident: contain first, explain second, never the other way around. In the first few minutes I'm not debugging the SSIS package line by line — I'm running the same row-count parity check we always run, source versus staging versus fact, scoped to last night's load window, because a revenue number that's roughly doubled screams either a join fan-out or a duplicate batch insert, and that check confirms which fast. Once I know the blast radius — is it just last night's incremental rows, or did it corrupt something further back — I make a call on containment, not a fix: can we roll back specifically last night's load, or do we point today's dashboard at yesterday's known-good refresh while we properly test the real fix? I will not let anyone push an untested patch into production an hour before a board meeting; that's trading one unverified state for another. On communication: I go to the executive stakeholders as soon as I have a confirmed scope and a safe number to present, not before I'm sure and not after I've quietly patched it. The message is always mitigation-first: 'we found an issue in last night's data load, it's isolated to [X], here's the number you can present with confidence, and we'll have the permanent fix validated by end of day.' Executives don't need the technical root cause at 8 AM — they need to know the number in front of them is trustworthy and that someone is already on it.
commonMistakes: Starts debugging ETL code line-by-line instead of running a fast scoping check first
Pushes an untested fix straight into production under time pressure
Tells the executive team either too early (before confirming scope) or too late (after silently patching)
Leads the exec conversation with root-cause detail instead of a safe number and a plan
Doesn't isolate whether the bug is scoped to last night's load or affects historical data too
keyPoints: Runs a fast, scoped diagnostic (row-count parity) before attempting any fix
Correctly reasons about join fan-out or duplicate-batch-insert as the likely cause of a doubled number
Chooses a safe containment action over an untested live fix under time pressure
Communicates to executives as soon as scope is confirmed, with mitigation-first framing
Separates 'what do we tell execs now' from 'how do we root-cause and fix permanently'

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Runs a fast, correct diagnostic approach under time pressure
Makes a sound containment decision instead of an untested live fix
Correct timing and content of executive communication
Demonstrates calibrated, confident incident leadership

questions.title: Diagnosing a Single-Source-of-Truth Violation Between SSRS and Power BI
questions.prompt: A plant manager reports that the SSRS paginated report and the Power BI dashboard, both reading the same warehouse, show different scrap rates for the same product and date range. Both tools are confirmed to point at the same server and database. Write the specific SQL cross-check you'd run first to isolate where the disagreement actually originates, and walk through the two or three most likely root causes this specific symptom points to, in order of likelihood.
questions.modelAnswer: With both tools confirmed to point at the same server and database, the bug is almost never in the warehouse itself — it's in a filter, date range, or expression difference between the two tools. The first move is to compute the business number directly from the warehouse with raw SQL, independent of either tool's own expression language, and treat that as the referee: if the raw SQL number matches one tool but not the other, the mismatched tool's expression or filter is the bug; if the raw SQL number matches neither, the problem is actually upstream in the warehouse data itself, which changes the whole investigation. In order of likelihood: first, a date range or filter mismatch — one tool filtering on EndDateKey and the other on a different date role (StartDateKey or DueDateKey), which is a textbook risk whenever a fact table has role-playing date dimensions. Second, a rounding or null-handling difference in how each tool computes the ratio — an SSRS expression dividing two integers versus a Power BI DIVIDE() measure that silently returns a blank instead of an error on a zero denominator, producing different results for edge-case rows. Third, and less likely once the first two are ruled out, a semantic model relationship or filter context issue in Power BI — an inactive relationship, or a slicer/visual-level filter the analyst didn't realize was applied — producing a result scoped differently than the SSRS report's parameter.
questions.professionalAnswer: Once I've confirmed both tools point at the same server and database, I stop trusting either tool's number and go straight to raw SQL as the referee — compute the scrap rate directly against the warehouse, independent of any DAX or SSRS expression, and see which tool it actually agrees with. That one query tells me whether this is a tool-side bug or a real warehouse data problem, which completely changes where I look next. My first guess, before I even run anything, is a date-role mismatch — this fact table has multiple date keys playing different roles, and it's a very easy mistake for one report to filter on EndDate while the other filters on DueDate without anyone noticing. After that I'd look at how each tool handles the division itself — a DAX DIVIDE() quietly returns blank on a zero denominator where a raw SSRS expression might error or return something else entirely, and that kind of edge-case handling difference is exactly the sort of thing that looks fine until you hit the one product with zero orders. Semantic model filter context is on my list too, but I check it last, because in my experience it's the least likely of the three once the server and database are already confirmed to match.
questions.example:
-- The referee query: compute scrap rate directly from the warehouse,
-- independent of either tool's own expression logic
SELECT
    p.EnglishProductName,
    SUM(f.ScrappedQty) * 1.0 / SUM(f.OrderQty) AS ScrapRateFromSQL,
    MIN(d.FullDate) AS RangeStart,
    MAX(d.FullDate) AS RangeEnd
FROM   dw.FactWorkOrder f
JOIN   dw.DimProduct p ON f.ProductKey = p.ProductKey
JOIN   dw.DimDate d    ON f.EndDateKey = d.DateKey   -- confirm this matches BOTH tools' date role
WHERE  p.EnglishProductName = @ProductName
  AND  d.FullDate BETWEEN @RangeStart AND @RangeEnd
GROUP BY p.EnglishProductName;
commonMistakes: Assumes the warehouse itself must be wrong without first running the raw-SQL referee check
Doesn't consider role-playing date dimension mismatch as a likely cause when a fact table has multiple date keys
Overlooks silent null/blank handling differences between a DAX measure and an SSRS expression on edge cases
Jumps to blaming one tool's bug before confirming which tool actually disagrees with the raw warehouse number
Doesn't check for an inactive relationship or hidden filter in the Power BI semantic model
keyPoints: Runs a raw-SQL cross-check as the referee before blaming either tool
Correctly identifies date-role mismatch as the most likely cause given role-playing dimensions
Identifies rounding/null-handling differences in ratio calculations as a real risk
Considers semantic-model filter context as a plausible but lower-likelihood cause
Reasons in order of likelihood rather than guessing at a single cause

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct, working referee SQL query
Correctly identifies date-role mismatch as most likely cause
Identifies at least one additional plausible root cause
Reasons in a sound, prioritized diagnostic order

questions.title: Architecture Review Board: Merging Six Regional Databases with Conflicting Customer Keys
questions.prompt: You're presenting to an architecture review board. A retailer is merging six regional databases into one enterprise warehouse. Each region has its own CustomerID numbering with real collisions (the same integer means different customers in different regions), and each region's customer dimension history was tracked inconsistently — some Type 1 only, some genuine Type 2, one region with no history at all. Existing regional reports must keep working throughout the migration. Walk through your end-to-end architecture: how you resolve the key collisions, your SCD strategy for the merged dimension, and how you sequence the migration so existing reports never go down.
questions.modelAnswer: Key collision resolution: the core principle is that regional CustomerIDs are natural keys, not globally unique identifiers, so the merged warehouse needs its own warehouse-generated surrogate key for every customer, and the natural key must be stored as a composite — (SourceRegion, CustomerID) — never the bare CustomerID alone, since the same integer legitimately refers to different people across regions. Every ETL lookup against the merged DimCustomer has to join on that composite natural key, not the regional ID in isolation; this is non-negotiable, because any lookup that forgets the region component will silently merge two different customers' facts together. SCD strategy for the merged dimension: because the six regions have inconsistent history (Type 1 only, genuine Type 2, and no history at all), the merged dimension cannot adopt one region's existing history as 'the truth' for all customers — instead, it needs attribute-by-attribute classification applied uniformly going forward (the hybrid SCD approach), with a pragmatic rule for backfilling: regions with real Type 2 history get that history preserved and loaded with real EffectiveDate/ExpirationDate values; regions with Type 1-only or no history get a single current row with EffectiveDate set to the migration cutover date, explicitly not fabricating history that was never actually tracked. This has to be documented and communicated — 'customers from Region C have no SCD history before this date' is an honest limitation, not a defect, and pretending otherwise by inventing dates would be worse. Migration sequencing for zero downtime: this runs as a strangler-pattern cutover, not a big-bang replace. Phase 1: build the merged warehouse alongside the existing regional systems, with ETL populating it from all six regions in parallel, while every existing regional report keeps reading its original regional source unchanged. Phase 2: validate the merged warehouse exhaustively against each region's existing numbers (the same row-count-parity and cross-tool-agreement checks used at smaller scale, run per region) until confidence is high. Phase 3: cut over reports one region at a time, repointing each region's reports to the merged warehouse only after that region's validation passes, so a problem discovered in region 4's migration doesn't block or break regions 1-3, which are already live on the new warehouse. Phase 4: decommission the old regional sources only after every region has been running clean against the merged warehouse for a defined stabilization period. At no point does an existing report go down, because nothing is repointed until its replacement is independently validated.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd walk the board through this in the order they'll actually push back on: keys first, because that's the landmine. Regional CustomerIDs collide by design — the same number means different people in different regions — so the merged warehouse needs its own surrogate key, and the natural key on the dimension has to be a composite of region plus the regional ID, never the bare ID alone. Every single ETL lookup has to honor that composite key, or we silently merge two unrelated customers' histories together, which is a far worse failure than any performance problem. On history: I'd be upfront that we can't invent SCD history that one region never tracked. My approach is a hybrid classification applied consistently from here forward, with real Type 2 history preserved where a region actually has it, and a clean 'current as of cutover' row where it doesn't — documented honestly, not backfilled with fabricated dates. On sequencing, I'd tell the board this is a strangler-pattern migration, not a cutover weekend: we build and validate the merged warehouse alongside the live regional systems with zero impact on existing reports, we validate region by region against each region's own known-good numbers, and we only repoint a region's reports once that region's validation passes — independently of how the other five regions are doing. That means if region 4 turns up a nasty edge case, regions 1 through 3 are already safely running on the new warehouse and unaffected. Nothing old gets turned off until everything new has been proven, region by region, for a real stabilization window.
commonMistakes: Treats regional CustomerID as globally unique and builds the merged dimension on it directly, guaranteeing silent data corruption
Picks one region's SCD history as 'the truth' and discards or fabricates history for the others
Proposes a big-bang cutover instead of a phased, per-region validated migration
Fabricates historical SCD dates for regions that never tracked history, instead of documenting the honest limitation
Doesn't propose region-by-region validation, risking one region's bug blocking or breaking all six
keyPoints: Identifies the composite natural key (region + regional ID) as the required collision fix
Designs a surrogate-key-based merged dimension with every lookup honoring the composite key
Proposes honest, non-fabricated SCD history handling per region's actual tracking history
Designs a phased, strangler-pattern migration sequenced to guarantee zero downtime
Validates each region independently before cutover, isolating risk

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly resolves the key collision with a composite natural key design
Designs a sound, honest SCD strategy across inconsistent regional history
Designs a genuine zero-downtime, phased migration sequence
Communicates tradeoffs and limitations honestly, not optimistically

questions.title: Architecture Review Board: Disaster Recovery Strategy for the Enterprise Warehouse
questions.prompt: The review board is asking for a disaster recovery strategy for the enterprise warehouse underlying SSRS and Power BI reporting for the whole business. There is currently no DR plan at all — a single SQL Server instance, no failover, no documented recovery procedure. Walk through the DR design you'd propose: what you'd protect first and why, your recovery time and recovery point objectives and how they differ for the warehouse versus the SSIS orchestration layer versus the Power BI semantic models, and the one operational practice that makes a DR plan actually trustworthy instead of theoretical.
questions.modelAnswer: A warehouse DR plan has to treat three layers differently, because they fail differently and recover differently. The data layer (the warehouse database itself, SSISDB, and the staging databases) is the highest priority to protect, because everything else is derived from it — SSRS reports and Power BI semantic models can be rebuilt or redeployed, but lost warehouse data (if the retention/backfill window has passed) may be unrecoverable. For this layer, I'd propose a defined RPO (how much data loss is tolerable — likely measured in hours, bounded by how often the nightly load runs and whether transaction log backups are taken between loads) and a defined RTO (how long the business can be without reporting before real harm — likely a business-day scale for this use case, not sub-minute, since this isn't a transactional system the business can't survive losing for a few hours). The concrete mechanism: regular full plus differential plus transaction log backups to a geographically separate location, with documented, periodically tested restore procedures — a backup nobody has ever restored from is not a DR plan, it's a hope. The orchestration layer (SSIS packages in SSISDB, SQL Server Agent job definitions) needs its own protection distinct from the data: these are configuration and code, best protected by keeping the project source (the .ispac-generating project) under source control and by scripting the Agent job definitions so they can be redeployed onto a recovered instance quickly, rather than relying on backing up SSISDB alone to carry job schedules. The Power BI layer is the lowest-priority, fastest-recovery piece, because the Service itself is Microsoft-managed infrastructure — the real DR requirement there is making sure the .pbix files and semantic model definitions are themselves under version control or backed up outside the Service, and that the Service's connection to the recovered warehouse is re-pointed (via Schedule refresh / gateway configuration) once the data layer is back. The single operational practice that makes any of this trustworthy rather than theoretical: scheduled, mandatory DR drills — actually restoring a backup to a separate environment and running the validation checklist (row-count parity, orphaned-key checks, cross-tool agreement) against the restored copy on a recurring cadence, not just writing the plan down once and filing it. A DR plan that's never been tested is a documented guess, not a capability.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd tell the board the honest baseline first: right now we have zero DR, which means any hardware failure or corruption event is an unbounded outage with unknown data loss, and that's the actual risk we're pricing in. My proposal treats three layers differently. The data itself — the warehouse, SSISDB, staging — is priority one, because it's the one thing that genuinely can't be quickly rebuilt if it's gone; I'd set an RPO in hours, tied to our load cadence and log backup frequency, and an RTO on the order of a business day, which is realistic for a reporting system the business can survive being without briefly, as opposed to a transactional system. That means full-plus-differential-plus-log backups shipped off-site, with a documented restore runbook. The orchestration layer — the SSIS packages and Agent jobs — I'd protect separately, through source control on the SSIS project and scripted job definitions, because that's config and code, not data, and it recovers differently. Power BI is the easy layer — Microsoft runs that infrastructure — our job there is just making sure our .pbix files are backed up outside the Service and that we have a clear re-pointing step once the warehouse is back. But I'd close by telling the board the part that actually matters most isn't any of that — it's that we commit to actually running a DR drill on a schedule, restoring to a real separate environment and validating it with our normal pipeline checks. A DR plan nobody has ever tested is a document, not a capability, and I don't want to find that out during a real incident.
commonMistakes: Proposes one blanket RTO/RPO for the whole system instead of differentiating by layer
Treats a backup existing as equivalent to DR readiness without ever testing a restore
Forgets the SSIS orchestration layer (jobs, packages) needs its own protection beyond the database backup
Assumes Power BI Service data needs the same DR treatment as the warehouse, missing that Microsoft manages that infrastructure
Proposes an unrealistically aggressive RTO/RPO for a reporting system that doesn't match the actual business cost of downtime
keyPoints: Differentiates DR treatment across the data, orchestration, and reporting layers
Proposes realistic, justified RTO/RPO values appropriate to a reporting (not transactional) system
Designs a concrete backup and restore mechanism for the data layer
Addresses source control / redeployment for the orchestration layer separately from data backup
Names scheduled, mandatory DR drills as the practice that makes the plan trustworthy

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly differentiates DR strategy across the three layers
Proposes realistic, justified RTO/RPO values
Designs concrete backup/restore and redeployment mechanisms
Identifies DR drills as the practice that validates the whole plan

questions.title: Mentoring a Junior Engineer Through a Flawed Dimension Design
questions.prompt: Tell me about a time you mentored a junior engineer through a code review where their design had a real conceptual gap — not a style issue. Use a specific scenario: a junior modeled a dimension as Type 1 (overwrite) when the business genuinely needed Type 2 history, and had already written the ETL before you caught it in review. Walk through it using the STAR method, including how you delivered the feedback and what you did about the already-written code.
questions.modelAnswer: Situation: a junior engineer on my team built out a Customer dimension's ETL load, and in code review I noticed CustomerSegment was being handled as a straight overwrite — Type 1 — while the business had explicitly asked for 'revenue by segment, historically' reporting that depends on knowing what segment a customer was in at the time of each order, which requires Type 2. The ETL was already fully written and had passed the junior's own testing, because their tests only checked that the current value updated correctly, not that history was preserved. Task: as the reviewer, my responsibility was both to stop an incorrect design from shipping and to turn this into a real learning moment rather than just a rejected pull request. Action: I didn't open with 'this is wrong.' I asked a question first — 'if a customer moves from Segment B to Segment A in March, and someone runs a segment revenue report for January, what should that report show?' The junior worked through it themselves and realized the overwrite would make every past order retroactively show the customer's current segment, silently rewriting history. That self-discovery mattered more than me just stating the rule, because they now understood the mechanism, not just the verdict. I then walked through the Type 1/Type 2 decision test with them directly against this attribute, and we agreed CustomerSegment needed Type 2 tracking while a couple of the dimension's other attributes, like PhoneNumber, correctly stayed Type 1. On the already-written code, I didn't just tell them to redo it alone — we paired on refactoring the load logic together, since converting a Type 1 load into a correct, transactional Type 2 UPDATE-then-INSERT pattern has real failure modes (I'd seen the surrogate-key and idempotency issues before) that were worth demonstrating directly rather than describing. Result: the corrected design shipped with real historical tracking, the junior caught a second Type 2 candidate attribute on their own during the refactor without me prompting it, and they referenced that same decision framework unprompted in a design review two months later for an unrelated dimension — which told me the lesson actually transferred, not just the fix.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd tell this one specifically because it's a good example of catching a conceptual gap, not a typo. A junior on my team had fully built a Customer dimension load with CustomerSegment handled as Type 1 overwrite, and the business need was explicitly historical segment reporting — which meant this was wrong at the design level, not the implementation level, and the code already worked, in the narrow sense that it ran without errors. In review, instead of just flagging it, I asked them to walk through what happens to a January segment report if a customer's segment changes in March under their design. They got there themselves — the report would silently show the customer's current segment applied retroactively to January's numbers, which is just wrong data dressed up as a working feature. From there we worked through the actual classification test together — does any report need this value exactly as it was at the time — and applied it properly across the whole dimension, not just the one attribute I'd flagged. Then we paired on rewriting the load as a proper transactional Type 2 pattern, because I wanted them to see the idempotency and surrogate-key details firsthand rather than just hear about them. The part I'm actually proud of: a couple months later, in an unrelated review, they independently applied that same test to a different dimension without me bringing it up. That's the actual measure of whether mentoring worked — not whether the one bug got fixed, but whether the reasoning stuck.
commonMistakes: Just states the correct answer to the junior instead of leading them to discover the flaw themselves
Fixes the code alone without involving the junior in the correction, losing the teaching opportunity
Focuses the story only on the technical fix with no Result beat describing what changed afterward
Treats this as a style/code-quality issue rather than a conceptual design gap
Doesn't address why the junior's own tests failed to catch the problem in the first place
keyPoints: Identifies this as a conceptual design gap, not a style nitpick
Uses a guided question to let the junior discover the flaw rather than being told
Pairs on the actual correction instead of just approving a redo
Applies the real SCD classification framework correctly to the specific attribute
States a concrete Result showing the learning transferred beyond the single incident

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Clear STAR structure with a concrete, specific scenario
Correctly diagnoses and explains the Type 1 vs Type 2 conceptual gap
Demonstrates effective, non-condescending mentoring technique
States a specific, credible Result beyond just 'it got fixed'

questions.title: Leading a Postmortem After a Disagreement with a Stakeholder Over Architecture Direction
questions.prompt: Tell me about a time you disagreed with a stakeholder over an architecture decision, and how you handled leading the postmortem after things didn't go the way you'd warned them about — or, if you prevented the problem, how you handled the disagreement itself while the stakeholder still outranked the decision. Use the STAR method, and be specific about how you communicated technical risk to a non-technical stakeholder.
questions.modelAnswer: Situation: a stakeholder wanted a new descriptive attribute (similar to the ShiftCode scenario from a late schema change) added directly onto a fact table as a raw text column, because it was faster to ship in the short term, overriding my recommendation to model it as a proper dimension with its own surrogate key. I explained the tradeoff clearly at the time — a raw text column on the fact table means any future rename or correction to that value requires updating every historical fact row instead of one dimension row — but the stakeholder prioritized the shipping deadline and the decision went their way. Task: my responsibility was twofold — ship what was asked for without silently sabotaging or slow-walking a decision I disagreed with, and be ready to lead the cleanup if the risk I'd flagged actually materialized. Action: I documented the tradeoff in writing at the time, not as a way to say 'I told you so' later, but so the decision and its known risk were traceable. Months later, the business did need to rename one of those category values across the board, and the predicted problem hit: a bulk UPDATE across millions of historical fact rows, with real risk of partial failure mid-update and no clean way to represent 'this category meant something different before this date' for historical reporting. I led the postmortem not by relitigating the original decision, but by walking the room through what happened, why it happened structurally, and the concrete fix: migrate the raw column into a proper dimension now, backfilling surrogate keys for historical rows, and correct the ETL to use the dimension going forward. I presented this to the same stakeholder in plain terms — not 'this proves I was right,' but 'here's what this is costing us now, here's the fix, and here's how we avoid paying this cost again.' Result: the stakeholder approved the dimension migration without resistance, because the cost was now concrete and visible rather than hypothetical, and we adopted a standing rule afterward that any new descriptive attribute gets a lightweight design review before landing on a fact table — which is now a real quality gate, not a verbal preference.
questions.professionalAnswer: I try to handle disagreements like this in two separate moments, and I'd tell this story that way. At the time of the original decision, my job wasn't to win the argument — it was to make the tradeoff completely clear and put it in writing, then respect that the stakeholder owns the business call even when I disagree with the technical direction. I recommended modeling a new category attribute as a proper dimension; they wanted it as a raw column on the fact table to ship faster, and I documented the risk — that renaming or correcting that value later would mean touching every historical fact row instead of one dimension row — and then I built it their way, because overriding a stakeholder's explicit decision after they've heard the tradeoff isn't my call to make unilaterally. Months later, when the business did need to rename a category value, that exact risk materialized, and I ended up leading the postmortem. I was deliberate about not making it an 'I told you so' conversation — nobody learns from that, and it burns trust I'd need again. Instead I walked through what broke, why it was structural rather than a one-off mistake, and the concrete remediation: migrate the column into a real dimension, backfill the history, fix the ETL. I brought the same stakeholder the fix with the cost made concrete instead of hypothetical, and they approved it immediately. The real result wasn't just fixing that one column — it's that we put a lightweight design-review gate in place afterward for exactly this class of decision, so the next disagreement gets caught before it ships instead of after.
